entry.title: My house has a chokehold over me!
entry.content:
and my perfect schedule does not stand a chance.

I had a plan for how I wanted to start October. My house had some inputs on said plan.

Things have been breaking around my house for the last couple of days. Extension cords shot, a water purifier out of action, and many electronics going through their moody teenage phase.

AArpit3 Oct

i have not checked the data, so don’t quote me on it.

A couple of days ago in Bangalore, we had what felt like the heaviest rain of the year. It started pouring in the evening, paused briefly, then returned for a thunderous night.

Anyway, September ended, and I am awake now – apparently for electrical repairs.

October felt important because life has been changing quite a bit for me lately. A while ago, I decided to step away from organising VizChitra after helping run the conference for two years. Also after two years, my role at work is evolving into a more favourable shape.

These changes have opened up a lot of time in my life, and I have been asking myself what I want my days to look like going forward and, most importantly, how to make room to create for myself again.

As a way to explore this creativity again, I have been reading The Artist’s Way with a friend and doing the weekly exercises (keep an eye out for the weekly series on it). I felt committed to October as the beginning of this shift in my life, with a little more space for myself to be.

Instead, the start of the month has been choppy and tiring. My house had its own plans for the month, and it did not feel like informing me about them.

I keep wanting to treat all of this like a regular interruption, fix what needs fixing, then get back to my day. But I am increasingly unsure that if one ever truly “gets back to their day.” while also inhabiting a house.

AArpit3 Oct

the constant anticipation.

There is always another fix waiting in the wings: a fan that starts clicking in the middle of a call, the cabinet hinge that suddenly wants to squeak. My attention has been permanently half-parked on just looking after the house for years.

I am not sure there was ever a stretch when the house didn’t need something. I cannot even remember many conversations from my childhood with my parents, where repairs were not a part of it.

And then there are the jobs I have invented for myself. My magnum opus is reorganising the bookshelf every six months. Either because the books on my shelves have changed, or the way I organise them in my head has shifted, so the bookshelf feels like it needs to reflect that.

Nobody is making me do that one. I just want the shelves to make sense again!

I could blame my current predicament on the limitations of this particular house, or maybe if I had more money for someone to take care of everything full-time I would not feel this. On a tiring day like the one I just had, both explanations are tempting.

But I love this house. I do not particularly want a bigger one. And I especially do not want to hand over all the looking after it, either. I like doing things myself, knowing where things are, deciding how they should work, making this place feel like mine.

I just wish it did not get so overwhelming sometimes.

Some of this feeling of being overwhelmed probably comes from how I plan my days. I fill them to the brim, assigning every available bit of time to something I want to do. There’s very little room for ambiguity. Certainly no slot labelled “water purifier not purifying”.

And when something breaks, I stop and deal with it – because that’s what living in a house requires, and because I care about this one.

I am tired at the end of all the fixes, and annoyed that I have not done what I planned, even though I have spent the day doing something that matters to me.

I do not have a neat conclusion, and not looking for solutions, either. Maybe I just want things to stop breaking for a while and catch a breath.

One thing I would appreciate is a significant amount of uninterrupted time reading, writing, or making things.

But I think I need to leave a little more room in my plans for the home I actually live in. Including the inconvenient parts of looking after it. I love this house. Sometimes I would like for it to love me back by keeping all its appliances working. For now, I will settle for a functioning water purifier.

entry.title: My Bangalore Food Map
entry.content:
Places I've eaten in Bangalore and whether they're worth another visit.

A little food notebook for Bangalore, collecting the places I’ve visited and rated out of five. I’ll keep adding to it as I eat my way through the city 😋

📝 Note: This is also an experiment, I might spin this into a separate maps collection.

Name Neighborhood Rating Note
Burma Burma Indiranagar ★★★★★ One of my all time favourites in the city. I've gone back multiple times. Lotus Biscoff Bubble Tea is a must!
Toit Indiranagar ★★★★★ Great food, great drinks, great vibe. One of my favourite places to hang out. Their english breakfast is a must.
Cafe Grey Indiranagar ★★★★★ Good food and ambience, affordable spot to work from. I'm a regular here.
Brott Indiranagar ★★★★½ Limited items and overhyped but their drinks are great. My favourite is the Coconut Cloud Coffee. Seating is cramped.
Beyondburg Indiranagar ★★★★☆ Expensive but good burger selection. Good for once in a while. I recommend the Smashstrami burger.
Brik Oven New Thippasandra ★★★☆☆ Overhyped but decent food. There are better places to eat in the area.
The Pizza Bakery Indiranagar ★★★★☆ Their garlic bread is a must try. Overall good pizza selection.
Rumi Indiranagar ★★☆☆☆ The dishes recommended by the staff were very bad. I don't recommend this place.
23rd Street Pizza Ashok Nagar ★★☆☆☆ All of the dishes were average at best. Skip this place.
Element 3 Indiranagar ★★★½☆ Great north indian pure veg restaurant. I really like their kofta curry.
Azuki Bistro Richmond Town ★★★★☆ The ambience, food and service are great. I recommend trying out their desserts.
Chin Lung Brewery Indiranagar ★½☆☆☆ Good for a bar scene but the food is below average. Go only if you want to get drunk.
Tandoori Taal Indiranagar ★★★☆☆ Some dishes are good but some aren't. I'll keep it in my list for the occasional visit.
Nagarjuna Indiranagar ★★★★☆ Nice andhra cuisine restaurant. Their biryanis are great.
California Burrito Indiranagar ★★★★★ A cult classic in the city. My favourite is the Chilli Chipotle Chicken Burrito.
Qissa Indiranagar ★★☆☆☆ Average food taste in terms of Mediterranean cuisine. I won't go back here.
The Fresh Factory Indiranagar ★★★★★ They have some really delicious and healthy food but very expensive. A must try though, try out their French Toast.
The Veg & Veg Indiranagar ★★★★☆ Regular after run breakfast spot. They have a nice selection of item.
Milano Pizza Indiranagar ★★★☆☆ Good for when you want to find something to eat at 12 AM. Their almond cake is good!
The Srirangam Cafe Indiranagar ★★★½☆ Biased but this is my goto spot for tea and snacks!
Pizza 4P's Indiranagar ★★★★★ Amazing food especially the burrata cheese pizza. Their tiramisu is my favourite!
Kake Di Hatti Indiranagar ★★★☆☆ Decent food for north indian cuisine. I don't go here anymore.
Kailash Parbat Indiranagar ★☆☆☆☆ I had a bad experience here including food poisoning. I don't recommend this place.
Foo Brigade Road ★★★★☆ Overhyped but good food. It's also very expensive, I'm taking 1 star off for that.
Bamey's Gastro Bar Koramangala ★★★★☆ Their food is amazing more so if you like Nepalese food. The jhol momos are a must try!
Truffles Indiranagar ★★★½☆ The sandwiches and pasta here are great. Good for a quick bite.
Umesh Refreshments Indiranagar ★★★☆☆ It's overhyped because of who has visited it. The food is average at best.
Cafe Muziris Indiranagar ★★★½☆ Another great spot for english breakfast. Do not get their pancakes though.
Zaitoon Kodihalli ★★★½☆ Their non veg dishes are great but veg not so much. The fusion dishes are a must try.
Kebapci Koramangala ★★★★★ Their kebabs are so good you'll want to eat them every day. A must try!
The Reservoire Koramangala ★★★★☆ The ambience and food is great along with live music. This one's better than Indiranagar.
Magnolia Bakery Indiranagar ★★★½☆ Their selection of desserts is great but the place is just too overhyped.
Good Flippin' Burgers Ashok Nagar ★★★☆☆ A good burger joint with a decent selection of burgers.
Khandani Rajdhani Indiranagar ★★★☆☆ Only go on Tuesdays for their rajasthani thali. The food is average.
Amicii Indiranagar ★★★½☆ Decent food but only go for the ambience and cocktails.
Bombay Brasserie Indiranagar ★★★☆☆ The food is nothing special but the place is unnecessarily expensive.
Chulha Chauki Da Dhaba Indiranagar ★★★½☆ The quantity is way too less for the price they charge. But the food is good.
Shyamji's Chole Bhature Koramangala ★★★★☆ I think these are the closest to Delhi I've had so far.
Offbeat Cafe Jayanagar ★★★★☆ Nice and small cozy cafe, I would go often if I lived nearby! They have some nice drinks 🍹
Bengaluru Cafe Jayanagar ★★★★☆ Great breakfast spot! I highly recommend visiting this.
Cafe Amudham Indiranagar ★★★☆☆ Their dosa was decent but tea was bad, maybe just a bad location :(
The Filter Coffee Indiranagar ★★★★★ Their menu and food is top tier, also a frequent spot for me. Highly recommend!
Beanlore Indiranagar ★★★½☆ I really liked the food here but the service was a bit weird. Try out their Hazelnut Latte!
Chaska Bun Indiranagar ★★★☆☆ Only go here for the Tea, Maska bun and vibes. There's no proper seating area and other items are pretty mid.
Byg Brewski Brewing Company Kaikondrahalli ★★★★☆ Great ambience and food but a pain to travel to :(
Bologna Indiranagar ★★★½☆ The food is good, but the portions don't justify the prices. Still worth visiting once in a while.
Cakewala BTM Layout ★★☆☆☆ I did not like both of the items I got. The cheesecake was so bad, I won't recommend this place.
MH12 Pavbhaji Indiranagar ★☆☆☆☆ Everything we ordered here was so bad! Please don't go here and waste your money.
Concu Indiranagar ★★★★☆ This is a great spot for co-working!
CK Vada Pav Indiranagar ★★★★★ Probably the closest to authentic vada pav and not charging exorbitant prices!
Nerlu Cafe Indiranagar ★★★★☆ The coffee and snacks are amazing here.
TWI (Taste Works) Indiranagar ★★★☆☆ This was decent, we had high hopes for Chole Bhature but it did not deliver. It's still not bad, worth it to try once.
The Bloom Cafe Jayanagar ★★★★☆ This place felt like we are in someone's home. The food and drinks were quite good, I'd definitely go back again!
Lavonne Ice Cream Kitchen Indiranagar ★★★☆☆ Naturals is way better, this place is overhyped!
Koreyaki Indiranagar ★★★½☆ The ramen is quite good here compared to most other places, deserves a visit!
Maffei Kitchen Koramangala ★★★★☆ The food here is delicious, a bit on the expensive side but totally worth it!
The Pump House JP Nagar ★★★★½ Just go for the ambience here! The food is also quite good but ambience tops it.
Chai Days Jayanagar ★★★½☆ Decent spot for late night snacks. I like their Vietnamese iced coffee.
The Hole In The Wall Cafe Koramangala ★★★★☆ Great spot for sandwiches and drinks, highly recommend.
IKEA Restaurant Bagalagunte ★★★☆☆ The meat balls that are so hyped are decent and overall food is average. They have some canned drinks which are nice though and are only available there.
Barkaas Whitefield ★★★★☆ The only thing you have to go for here is their Mandi!
Hallimane Restaurant Malleshwaram ★★★★☆ The food here is great, we went for their special mango meal which is seasonal. Definitely worth trying out once!

entry.title: The Impossible Bucket List
entry.content:
The Impossible Bucket List

This post was created during the Indie Web Club BLR meetup on 2026-10-03 based on the writing prompt "My impossible bucket list"

Visiting the family ancestral home

I have grown up hearing stories about the homes our family had until two generations ago in the villages we come from. Large agricultural plots with paddy fields being harvested and stored in massive wooden grain boxes that were larger than a metropolitan bedroom. Stories of my grandparents growing up there and getting up to mischief with others in town or parents going over there from the city for summer vacations and getting together with extended families. Often 15-20 people would stay together at the house, mattresses rolled on the floors and yet spacious enough for twice as many people.

However, none of these exist anymore. The buildings are gone, the farmland is split up between other families and everything in the house got sold except for tiny pieces of memorablia distributed sparsely between hundreds of relatives.

I often hear my mother still pining for the large brass (I think) cooking cauldrons and pots that would be used to cook for the entire crowd of ravenous kids and gossiping parents over open wood fires; the smell of the wood itself permeating into the rice and gravies in a way that we never get to experience these days. I do wish I could experience all of this firsthand and not just from memories as even these second-hand stories will end with our generation, unable to pass it on with any of the passionate remembrance of our elders' experiences.

Getting lost

The experience of being lost, truly lost, without knowing where you are, how to get out of the location, knowing the local language, or knowing how things work in an unfamiliar environment is kind of lost to us in the current generation.

I could be walking to the same place I have visited every month for a year and still pull out a maps application on my smartphone to know exactly how many metres or minutes to the destination. I could be in a country unable to read the script or understand a single spoken word and still communicate entirely through a translator app, or worse, an AR smartglass which puts subtitles over people in real life.

But I still miss the joy of navigating those challenges before it became so trivialized, the small wins from knowing all the turns in and out of narrow alleyways that led you through a slightly shorter route or using the wind and sun to figure out which direction to head to instead of the map app.

I sometimes actively put these constraints on myself when exploring but it's not quite the same experience knowing the safety net we have now with technology.

Cataloging every object at home

This is technically possible, but practically impossible.

Having a process and system that lets me track an inventory of every book, document, roll of tape or spoon in the house. Where the item is, where they came from, when was it purchased or received?

I have terrible memory, and yet I sometimes want to know things about the "stuff" in my house that I just practically could never.

How old is this pant? (also why do they not put at least a year of manufacture in clothes?)

Do I already have the eighth Wheel of Time book?

Where is the stapler (and do I actually own a stapler)?

The experience of experiencing something incredible for the first time, but every time

The first time I went SCUBA diving, the first time I had pizza in Europe or ramen in Tokyo. The taste of sambar after a year in Hong Kong.

I can never experience these things for the first time again, but sometimes it would be incredible to feel that rush again.

The energy of my grandparents

My grandparents have maintained their neverending energy and inspiring will to live well into their 90s. For someone who was born in the 1920s, my grandfather still has this youthfulness that is inspiring, endearing and just impossible to comprehend. Their ability to withstand pain and extend love to others is something I can only hope to achieve.

entry.title: IndiaFOSS 2026
entry.content:
IndiaFOSS

Attended my first indiafoss event. It's not my first FOSS conference(was even at FOSDEM2017 but that feels like a different era entirely) and definitely not my first tech conference.

Community

So glad to bump into people I've met briefly at various events and places again. This event brought together a lot of different circles with like minded folk. I'm not actively a part of the "tech community" in the city so this isn't my normal experience attending other events or workshops.

Shout out to Indie Web Club and Paper Crane Labs, I've only attended each once but the people made me feel at home even in the throngs of folk waiting to chime in with their take on AI (both for and against) at the drop of a free debian sticker.

I work at a company that's only brought up in conversation as a piece of nostalgic history so it was a bit of a pleasant surprise to bump into and connect with a colleague outside of the office.

Talks

I didn't attend too many of the talks but there were so many that looked incredibly interesting.

Some of the ones that stuck:

Day 1:

  • @qaree.bi's very cool work building music equipment as Tarab Instruments. Practical suggestions on getting started, a relatable story on going from hobby to business and the pains of soldering with a cheap iron.
  • Azan's strudel.cc workshop. I lugged around my laptop all day just for this and it was super fun. I have experimented briefly with TidalCycles and SuperCollider a long time ago but forgot so much of it since.
  • Tracking-free and hackable network cameras by Abhas Abhinav. I have worked in this domain for years, so ideas i am familiar with but cool to see others in the same space doing very interesting work.

Day 2: Spent most of the time in the design room

  • https://sanchaya.org/ has done really cool work with analyzing and reconstructed kannada typography from scanned books(they're using a slightly modified version of the Internet Archive's design to scan books nondestructively)
  • bezier curves are cool as heck
  • purchased a CoryDora macropad with no idea what I'm going to do with it. I think I'm team Brown keyswitches but not yet fully converted to mechanical keyboards for regular use.

My limited social battery ran out early on day 2 but had some wonderful conversations with folk on topics ranging from capturing the sounds of nature for science to open water swimming and a long attempt at figuring out what Frappe actually does.

Having attended Open Source India last year which is a corporate ad-filled and enterprise AI driven yapmare, this was actually enjoyable and embraced the community spirit of the open source multiverse.

Can't wait to spend weekends working on projects again!

entry.title: My Impossible Bucket List
entry.content:
1. Witness first contact with Aliens

In the summer of 2019, I was visiting Bir, helping organise Hillhacks. It’s great fun - You talk tech, art and policy in the day, and sit next to a campfire in the night, perhaps with some “fresh” Rice mead.

One night, while lying alone in the grass, next to a campfire that I was failing to ignite, I noticed a bright dot in the sky, moving across the horizon.

I was a big airplane nerd at this point in life. I knew this was no airplane. The color was wrong. This light was too bright. There was no blink. There were no trails. The lights were too high up for the elevation I was at. Maybe military jets?

I was also a budding space nerd too then. Perhaps this was a satellite - I hadn’t seen one yet, but I knew that in the right place at the right time, you could see satellites or the ISS in the sky, as their solar panels reflect sunlight back to earth. Maybe this is me witnessing my first satellite.

Tidbit: The correct time is just after sunset, or just before sunrise. The correct place is a place with very little light pollution.

It only took me 5 seconds to go through all those thoughts, when I noticed another bright dot following the first dot. Then another. Then another.

Within 30 seconds, there were 20+ bright dots channelling across the sky. In a perfect line with perfectly even spacing.

This is it. I am here. It’s happening. The world is going to be different from this moment on. Everything we knew is going to change. Everything we care about is going to be different. Humanity’s next adventure starts now, and I am here for it.

I go to google news straight up, expecting this to be the first story. Nothing.

Ok, this has just happened, maybe under a minute ago. Give people a chance to write it first, and then for Google News to pick it up.

But twitter is instant news, isn’t it? I go to twitter, and search ‘ALIENS’. Nothing.

WTF. I search ‘Sky’. Nothing. I search ‘Space’.

SpaceX successfully launches 60 satellites at once.

Fuck you Elon.

This was written as a writing prompt at IndieWebBlr.

entry.title: Fix nested Emacs frames
entry.content:
Earlier this year I added Ghostel to my Emacs configuration. Ghostel is a terminal emulator for Emacs that uses Ghostty's engine underneath. It is a delight to use especially with the TUI applications.

Nested Emacs frame problem

I use Emacs in daemon mode, and then use emacsclient to open new frames from the daemon. To use the same Emacs daemon when opening files through other programs such as git, sops, I have a small shell script ee configured as my default EDITOR. It opens a new Emacs frame in the terminal.

#!/bin/sh

exec emacsclient --create-frame --no-window-system "$@"

When I run this script from Ghostel, it opens a nested Emacs frame in Ghostel's terminal session.

Solution

Emacs sets an environment variable INSIDE_EMACS for shells and subprocesses. The script use this variable to check if it is launched from Ghostel and use the --reuse-frame flag to open the new buffer in the current frame.

#!/bin/sh

if [ "$INSIDE_EMACS" = "ghostel" ]
then
  exec emacsclient --reuse-frame "$@"
fi

exec emacsclient --create-frame --no-window-system "$@"

entry.title: Battle of the Chai Premixes
entry.content:
Hello! I like chai a lot, as you might know. I also like making it; as soon as I learned how to grate adrak and boil milk, I became the staple person to make chai for the family. It could just be that no one else wants to do it, but I like to think it’s because I make it so well. :P ¶

Ever since I shifted to hostel though, getting my hands on a stove and a boiler has been… “difficult” might be an understatement. The hostel declared that stuff as basically illegal. But I’ve had to look for many alternatives to get that same satisfaction that I get after a sip of hot chai. So far, the only solution I’ve reached is chai premixes. ¶

I’ve tried many of them on and off throughout hostel. I remember there were times I grimaced at the taste of the chai or even greatly enjoyed it, but I never really kept track of which ones I liked/disliked. Now that I’ve graduated, I feel like I have an obligation to reach a conclusive staple, for my own future grocery runs. So let’s do that. ¶

For both our sakes though, I’m not going to italicize chai for the rest of the post. We both know I’m referring to tea, so let’s keep it that way. This is also a good place to point out that none of these brands sponsored me; I meticulously spent my own money every 15 days when a premix box ran out. :P ¶

Namaste Chai

This was one of my favourites in college, and I was worried I’d set some high expectations if I started with this one. But it was already in my inventory, so I proceeded with testing it. ¶

Namaste Chai always has a very strong aroma for every flavour. You might find this too much, but I personally found it calming as I had chai after a long day of classes/work. I have no idea which company they originate from (I’m writing this while sitting in an IndieWebClub Meetup, so I can’t really check the box), but the aesthetic is all very cool anyway. ¶

They have one of the largest catalogs on this list, including — apart from “Kadak”, “Cardamom” or “Masala” chai — Lemongrass chai. Like what even? I remember ordering this flavour by accident in college, and making a face at the smell at the start. But by the time the packet ended I actually kinda enjoyed it. I haven’t been able to find presently though, so that hunt continues. ¶

Their sachet size is the largest on this list; around 22 grams. This is good for adding for flavour to each cup which I enjoy, but it also means there’s more total sugar in each sachet, if that’s something you’re concerned about (around 11 grams in each, to be specific). ¶

The taste itself though is one of the best. I come back to this brand time and again, and their variety has kept me a semi-loyal customer. ¶

Chaayos

If you’ve ever used chai premixes, this is probably the brand that comes to your mind first. Chaayos I feel has had a large impact on the café scene in India, particularly because of their, ¶

  1. very, very custom chai ingredient choices,
  2. the desi vibe which makes them feel more at-home compared to Western establishments, and
  3. a pretty large collection of things that you’d commonly eat with chai.

Chaayos is also a relatively expensive place, which makes them more like an Indian version of Starbucks, but I digress. We were talking about chai premixes. ¶

The first premix I used was from Chaayos, because my mom got it delivered from Amazon. The branding was all very cool and I remember liking it at the time too. But I think it’s because of the variety that I ended up getting a low-sugar variant by accident, didn’t like it, and decided to set out on my own premix discovery. So in a way they are to be thanked for this post. ¶

The premix from the above picture was my first Chaayos trial. It included three variants, and all three of them were… fine? The taste and notes were less distinct than I remember them being, so that was a little disappointing. ¶

One thing to note is that most of these premixes have sugar to premix ratio that’s around 1:2. So half of the premix is just sugars, which was the case here too (7 grams in 14 grams of premix). But the sugar here was much less distinct compared to Namaste Chai. ¶

I also have biscuits with my chai, specifically “Sunfeast Farmlite Oats & Chocolate”. So the sugar from those is bound to overpower the sugar from the chai. But I still usually notice it while drinking this one, which I usually do. ¶

This is the other premix of theirs I tried, which for some reason only comes in a Pack of 4 (and was covered in oil when I ordered it from Blinkit). I liked this one a lot more because the presence of adrak was noticeable, and felt a lot more like chai at home. Still though, these premixes are relatively expensive. ¶

Red Label

I kinda like Red Label as a brand, in a purely aesthetic sense. I mentioned in a previous blogpost that our family was trying out their chaipatti as an alternative to Taj Mahal, which is still an experiment in progress. But I was excited to have their chai premix anyway. ¶

After making the first cup and drinking it without an accompaniment (biscuits or otherwise), I was left frowning at my mug. The colour and smell were fine, but the taste itself felt like it was artificially sweetened. Which is when I looked at the information and the box and went, “Ah.” ¶

The concoction tasted how those yellow SugarFree™ powders used to smell, and the experience got a little worse when having it with biscuits that had real refined sugar, because the made the chai taste weird. I was disappointed with this one overall. ¶

Tata Tea Gold

This one, much like Red Label, came across my radar as a brand that makes normal chaipatti but is expanding to other forms of chai. The packaging was very cool and I liked the colours, now I just had to boil some water and taste it. ¶

The taste was okay, and the different notes battle a little bit to stand out, but I think there’s something wrong with this one? The chai itself was nice and masala-y, and didn’t have any noticeable amount of sugar. But every time I’d make this chai, I noticed a ring of red residue left at the top of the mug. ¶

I’ve made sure it’s not something that was already in the mug. From what I’ve observed though, it’s the foam from the premix that first starts out orange and then later on shifts to red. I don’t know if this points to how real or synthetic the premix is, but I’m probably not going to buy this one again. Ever. ¶

Also the premix, per calculation, contains about 7 grams of sugar for every 14 gram serve. I couldn’t for the life of me taste any reasonable sugar inside the thing though. ¶

Girnar Instant Tea

This is one that I got after trying everything else, just to make sure I’d gone through all my options. I relate Girnar to railways for some reason? Like I expect this chai to be served when travelling on the train. But I don’t know why, Girnar seems more like an afterthought to me when considering chai premixes. ¶

I, once again, accidentally got the low sugar variant here and wasn’t happy with it. I don’t even know if they have a normal sugar one. I tried adding honey to it which was okay, but I’d like to give this one a fair shot again with a proper amount of jaggery/sugar. Until then, this is not the one. ¶

I was having chai on the balcony for this last one, grimacing at the taste. I was just waiting for the mug to finish when one of my neighbours dropped in and we started chatting. It was normal stuff about work and weekends, but I noticed that the chai started tasting better over the course of the conversation. That was interesting. ¶

I don’t want to end this post on a cheesy “the real good chai was the friends we made along the way,” though. So I’ll instead be childish and just declare an objective winner that I prefer personally. ¶

That winner for me, in this post, is Namaste Chai. Remember how I was foreshadowing that I don’t want to set high expectations for the rest of the premixes? It looks like I did. And I’m fine with the slightly higher sugar content I think, because the chai is good enough that I feel satisfied and don’t crave another one for a while. So that’s that. ¶

I’ll continue to experiment with newer ones from time to time though. For example, none of the premixes mentioned here were dairy-free, so I’m keen to look for something in that department. None of these are a replacement for chai by any means, and some of them are probably even using artificial colours to look like chai. But the sloppy imitation will suffice for now. ¶

By the way, this draft started originally on 31st May, 2026. So it has been in the works for a loong time. Very glad I finally published, and this post is dedicated to all the people I have been telling about “this thing I’m doing” for weeks. :)

entry.title: Denden: Emacs Lisp SSG based on org-publish
entry.content:
Denden is yet another SSG based on org-publish and utilizing complete Elisp ecosystem. This site is built using that. Its not a package per-say, just an helper and building blocks on top of org mode's native ox-publish and org-element for AST.

Why I even started this

This site used to run on Hugo using same theme called hakimacs, with content in Org mode rendered through go-org, and it worked fine for months. But I hated looking how ugly go-template looked and lot of regexp to do something, although it was fast, it was not human (emacs user) friendly to read at all. When I wrote in org mode, I always liked why not elisp somewhere to hack and do stuff. Org is a rich ecosystem and it needs way more hackable place to configure, not hugo to regexp parse everything.

Org has a perfectly good parser living right inside Emacs, org-element, that turns any .org file into a proper tree I can walk, query, and reshape however I like. So the question became obvious, why am I throwing that tree away and going back to regexing strings, when the real structure is sitting right there the whole time.

That annoyance is the entire reason denden exists.

What denden actually is, and isn't

denden is not a package, its more like a tool, helpers and building block on top of org-publish. It uses all native org mode libs and org-publish, the publishing engine that already ships inside Org mode, plus a small pile of Elisp helper functions sitting on top of it, that's the whole thing. denden.el itself is one file, no hidden layers, no magic you can't just M-x describe-function your way into. 

;; this is roughly the entire mental model
(require 'denden)
(setq denden-content-directory "~/my-site/content")
(setq denden-publishing-directory "~/my-site/public")
(setq denden-full-build-function #'my-site-build)
;; now M-x denden-build just works

Everything else, feeds, sitemap, search index, OG card images, the accessibility linter, is a building block you call when you want it, not a framework deciding things for you. If you don't like how I did sitemaps, you just don't call denden-sitemap-xml, and write your own three lines instead. Nobody's stopping you, there's no true "denden way" to acheive it.

Templates are just lists, the sexp-HTML bit

This is the part I like the most, a denden template is not a template language at all, it's a plain Emacs Lisp list, shaped like this. 

(TAG ATTRIBUTE-PLIST . CHILDREN)

A tag symbol, a plist of attributes, then however many children you want, which can themselves be more nodes or plain strings. Something this small turns into real HTML. 

(list 'div '(:class "card")
      (list 'h2 nil "Hello")
      (list 'p '(:class "muted") "Written as a list, not a string template."))
;; C-x C-e => (div (:class "card") (h2 nil "Hello") (p (:class "muted") "Written as a list, not a string template."))

Run that through denden-serialize-node and you get. 

<div class="card"><h2>Hello</h2><p class="muted">Written as a list, not a string template.</p></div>

No Jinja-style <% if %> tags, no template DSL to look up in some docs page, it's Lisp, so it's just Lisp. If you need a loop you use mapcar, if you need a condition you use if, you already know how, because you already know Emacs Lisp, or you're learning it anyway for your config.

Here's a tiny real one, lifted straight from denden's own example site, denden/example/example-theme.el, the page header. 

(cl-defun example-theme-header (&key site-title menu-items)
  "The page header: SITE-TITLE linking home, then a MENU-ITEMS nav."
  (list 'header nil
        (list 'a '(:class "title" :href "/")
              (list 'h2 nil site-title))
        (append (list 'nav nil)
                (mapcar (lambda (item) (list 'a (list :href (cdr item)) (car item)))
                        menu-items))))

That's a whole working nav bar, menu-items is just a list of (label . url) pairs. Add a link to your site, add one more cons cell, no shortcode, no registering a new partial, nothing to restart.

How my own site is built with it

My site's own Elisp lives in exactly three files, and I think that's a feature, not something I need to apologize for.

  • denden/denden.el : the generic core engine, nothing specific to my site at all.
  • site/site.el : my config and page logic, menu items, badges, feed setup, everything that's my data.
  • theme/theme.el : my actual sexp-HTML templates.

Config is just Elisp data, so it looks like this, shortened from my real site.el. 

(defconst site-menu-main
  '((:name "Home" :url "/")
    (:name "Blog Posts" :url "/log/")
    (:name "Wander My Small Web" :url "/wander/")
    (:name "Media" :url "/media/")
    (:name "Quotes" :url "/quotes/")))

Want another nav item, add a line. Want a new badge on my footer, same deal, it's one more plist in a list, no new file, no new template syntax to learn.

Everything you're reading right now, the , the , the Wander My Small Web, the Pose | Vivre Card quick-thought cards, the accessible dialogs, all of that is just more sexp nodes and a bit of plain JS, sitting on top of the same three files.

One more cool bit, even the OG card images are sexp

OG cards, the preview image you see when a link gets shared on social media, are usually generated with some headless browser screenshot setup or an image library. In denden it's the exact same (TAG ATTRIBUTE-PLIST . CHILDREN) trick, just aimed at <svg> instead of <div>, from my own site.el.

I know IK, by now you might realize and say this is hard to write as well, but thats the cool stuff. Own it in lisp way. Direct maintenance of HTML files with no system is also cool tho ;-) 

(list 'svg (list :xmlns "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" :viewBox "0 0 1200 630"
                  :width "1200" :height "630" :font-family "Code D OnePiece, monospace")
      (list 'rect '(:width "1200" :height "630" :fill "#000000"))
      (list 'rect '(:width "1200" :height "68" :fill "#0a0f0a"))
      (list 'text '(:x "100" :y "46" :fill "#5fd7af" :font-size "30" :font-weight "bold")
            card-site-title)
      ;; ... and so on, title lines, tags, excerpt, favicon, all the same nodes
      )

Same denden-serialize-node (check file) call at the end, except this time the string it hands back is an SVG file sitting at /log/some-post/og.svg. No separate image-generation step, no Canva template, just more rects and text nodes.

It's also properly fast

I was bracing for a slow first build, since Emacs isn't exactly famous for being a speed train. It wasn't. A full build of this entire site, every post, every feed, every OG card image, finishes in a couple of seconds. I build it from the terminal like this. 

emacs --batch -Q -L denden -L site -L theme \
    -l denden/denden.el -l site/site.el -l theme/theme.el \
    --eval '(setq denden-repository-directory "/path/to/my/site")' \
    --eval '(site-build t)'

That's a cold batch Emacs, loading three files, building every page from scratch since t skips the incremental cache, and it's done before switch two windows. There's also an async build mode and a timestamp cache for day to day editing, so normal single-file saves rebuild near instantly through denden-preview-current-file.

Owning the whole thing

The thing I like most isn't the speed, it's that I own every line of this. I'm an Emacs user, I already spend my May I Recommend EWM tweaking my config, and now my blog engine runs in the same language, the same editor, the same muscle memory. If I want a new feature, I don't wait for a plugin, I don't learn a templating DSL, I just write a function next to the ones already there and call it. That's a genuinely different feeling from configuring a static site generator, it's closer to how your Emacs config itself grows over the years, one small function at a time, shaped around what you personally want.

If any of this sounds interesting and you're also an Emacs plus Org mode person, go have a look at denden bearblog example site. There's a small, complete example site in the repo example/ directory, a Bear-Blog-style site with a home page, an about page, a blog listing and a couple of posts, one stylesheet, no JavaScript. You can build and serve it yourself with one command, just example-build or just example-serve from inside denden/, and poke around the two small files that make it tick, example-site.el and example-theme.el, to see the whole pattern in one sitting, before you even think about pointing it at your own content.

Snap of a example bearblog like site built with denden

About the name

A denden mushi is the snail-shaped transponder phone from One Piece, the way everyone in that world talks to each other across the sea. If you've looked around this site even a little, the One Piece theme is not exactly subtle here. A static site generator's job is carrying your words from your Org files out to the rest of the world, felt fitting enough that I didn't look for a second name, although I did consider "dennow" to mimic "Then & Now", alas something had to stay.

Give it a spin, and if you build something with it, I'd genuinely like to hear about it.

entry.title: IndiaFoss 2026
entry.content:
I attended India FOSS this past weekend. This is a log of what happened basically.

Day 0

Had some potential conflicts in the morning so I sadly missed the P5.js workshop I had signed up for. But then I got to attend the OCaml workshop. It was conducted by the people at FP Launchpad. While I have been learning a bit with OCaml, this was a very good refresher. I have some experience with Haskell, so the syntax didn't trip me. But it is always interesting to see other people come into contact with Functional programming. You go to a beginner workshop, and people ask interesting questions.

For example, OCaml has a feature wherein a recursive function defintion has a rec keyword before it. 

let rec factorial n =
  if n = 0 then 1
  else n * (factorial (n-1))

Why is that? Haskell doesn't it for example. A function is a function is function , right? Turns out it's because the OCaml compiler allows you to define multiple functions with the same name. And so if the rec keyword is not specified, it will refer to a previous function's definition, not the one we intend. So in the same program, if for some reason you want to define a function named factorial, you can do so. Haskell does not allow you to do this.

Or for example, why is the let keyword everywhere? Isn't this a bit confusing to read. Somebody asked that question. Not a bad point actually. You get used to these things if you work with functional languages. But to people who are new, the friction points are very obvious. So that was very cool to see.

The workshop was great! I am doing a project in OCaml now and it's helping. So, thank you to Alina, Kaustubh, Smayan and Vimala (and anyone else I might have missed) for conducting it and answering all of our questions patiently.

Day 1

Onwards and upwards. I went for Prof KC's talk again on teaching OCaml in an interactive manner. It was a very good talk. The questions section was something else. Prof KC had mentioned that he used LLMs to build a bulk of the interactive book. So one person in the audience did something I never imagined. He asked, in the most straightforward manner "I really love teaching, but now I feel that with LLMs, I will not be able to tell my students the value of learning. Teaching is being taken away from me."

I have attended a lot of technical talks at many meet-ups. Bangalore is full of them. But never in my life have I seen someone ask a question that vulnerable. He was not saying "This is how I get my money, and it is being taken away." He was not angling to look smart, to out-think the speaker or to get attention. He was simply saying "I love doing this, it is being taken away from me and that makes me sad." Not because that was his livelihood. But because teaching was an end in and of itself for him. Sincerity? In this economy? Insane. The question was also answered thoughtfully - "For the students who want to learn, the good way of teaching will still be valuable." And in the span of that interaction, I realised something was different about this event. Put a pin on it.

Walked around a bit. And then I met Kajal from the WE program. The WE program, I have written about it here before. Kajal is one of the "usual suspects" as Asokan would say, who comes to our regular Sunday meetups. I recognised her and went to say hi. Good decision past me. She was volunteering for the event, along with her friend Navya. Over the course of event, these two girls just adopted me basically. I got to have lunch in the special section because I was with them. Ha! Seated lunch in a nice-ish secluded spot, oh the joys of life.

More importantly, I saw that there was a Community-Con. This was going to be a 10 minute talk selected based on votes from attendees. Now my CFPs had been rejected twice from IndiaFOSS. So I didn't have many hopes. I talked to both of them, and they were kindly encouraged me to apply. I was still a bit unsure, but I managed to propose a talk. Put a second pin on it.

Hardware! There was a separate section for the hardware products. They had a tiny robot on that was holding a brush, dipping it in paint, and then working on a canvas. Crazy. And there were startups selling PCB software. There was a lab by students from Ashoka university, where they had 3D printed the Kanchenjunga mountains. Gorgeous stuff. Saw a random girl just moving around in a makeshift car. Good for her.

The Cool Painting Robot

A crowd pleaser

IndiaFOSS has the genius idea to do Devroom by other communities. In DevRooms, the independent community organisers handle everything. I was mostly hanging out in the compilers Devroom only. AJ from FP India did a talk on strong static types and why they are important. It was great, but I know him, so I knew it would be great. Again, people were asking actually good questions. What was happening?

Hazy Picture of the overcrowded Compilers Devroom

I then went to attend Varuni's (again fellow WE program alumni) birds of a feather session on diversity. This was a really really good session. It was about what communities can do beyond just grants for encouraging diversity. Varuni, Ruchika and Suchitra, shoutout to them truly. The session was informal, but had a good structure. People were able to speak quite frankly about their troubles. Especially now, in this time when EDI has become less fashionable. And the consequences of that in their lives.

They had the brilliant idea towards the end, that each person would take two post-it notes. On one, write down an opportunity you can open the door for. Could be anything, but something you can help someone else with. And on the other, something you need help with. Some opportunity you are looking for. I was a bit worried i'd not have any opportunities to give. But then people started giving small ones. Like helping with reviewing CFPs to programs you have been accepted to. Then I was able to think of some things which I could help someone else with. And boy if that isn't a good feeling.

Day 2

Went a bit late to day 2. It was a Sunday but the place was still packed. I had prepared since the previous night for my proposed talk. I wasn't sure if I'd be selected, results would be announced later. But we hope for the best, and prep for the worst. I spoke to the people at SciPy India. The people from Paper crane labs who made some very cool visualisations. I have been to their lab and done laser cutting. But still it was amazing to see the some of this stuff.

And then the time came for results. My talk had been selected. Who these 41 people were who voted for me, I have zero clue. But thank you to them. So I went and prepared some more. I was quite nervous. Again, Kajal and Navya graciously offered to help me prepare. As much as I could within an hour.

I met the wonderful Niya during the event. We kept crossing paths throughout. She recommended a talk by the head of Data for India. She does data journalism. This was quite interesting. The government publishes a lot more data than I realised. Which is it's own can of worms. I have been reading the work of Robert Caro. Will write about it some other day. But basically Robert Caro is an autobiographer who digs deep. He will find out the exact amount a civil servant took as a bribe in 1922. But one thing he mentions is that these facts, while they exists, they are also a story. The truth does not come unadorned. And she spoke quite beautifully, very frankly. She was calm and poised. And her task is to present that data. But keep it as close to the source of the truth, while telling a story. Not easy at all. Great work.

Community Con

There were 7 community talks selected. One of them was Kailash Nadh, CTO of Zerodha! I had spoken to him on Day 1. He was quite thoughtful. His talk was amazing. But how am I supposed to go after him? Half the people in the hall left after him. Which, I confess, relieved me a bit. Regardless I was quite nervous. This was a main hall, it was huge. But I tried to remain calm.

There was a talk before me on running linux on phones by Shantanu Khedkar. It was great! I later found out that he is in 11th grade! Crazy! So smart. He is going places.

And then I gave my talk. It was basically the previous blog. But I tried to demo everything I could. I could have done a better job I think. While I was able to present a story of the zombie apocalypse I missed the main point. Distributed by default? That was the question I asked in the beginning. But did not answer properly. Elixir/Erlang programs don't care about where your node is. As long as it's resolvable, they will run communicate. That is the point.

Regardless, a nice photo from the talk. Zombie picture credits to Fred Hebert.

And a thank you to AJ from FPIndia for this photo.

I left soon after. Let us remove the first pin. The reason this event worked was that there was a good mixture of things being discussed, with a good spirit that too. On the one hand there are technical sessions, then there are session on data journalism. A strudel session! People were genuinely excited for the talks. I saw people looking at their phone calendars, jumping from hall to hall. I think that the less corporate feel of the event was probably one of the reasons. There were mostly students there. Which probably contributed to the feel of "college techfest but for adults."

Companies were present, but they did not take over the event. I recall one of the sponsors telling me that sponsorship did not result in a "reserved" speaking spot. It probably leads to a bias in speaker selection. But it's still not handed over to a company. The CFPs are open for all. And while they have a likes based system I am not a big fan of, the likes don't guarantee a speaking slot. People with very few likes also got to speak. The event network, was frankly better than other much bigger hackathons and events I have gone to, was setup by a bunch of kids from NITK. They had to lug the kilos of cable around. God bless them.

But it was really fun. I will be a repeat customer. Hopefully, see you all next year!

Post Notes

I went to one of the booths, and there, met a person from my college. So naturally I started singing the song. NMI - he cut me off and said in a beleagured voice, "Please. Don't.". So it goes.

Once, at a separate conference, a wonderful person who shall remain unnamed was with me. They saw the word OCaml written somewhere and said oh "Orange County Association of Machine Learning". And then some researcher SLOWLY turned around and looked at them with a what I imagine was just a "Whattt are you saying?" glare. So in my heart it is always OCaML.

After my talk, some people came up to talk to me about FP! So that is great. Most importantly, some people from FP India actually gave me constructive feedback. That was great! Was able to fix some things in the previous blog. Grateful to all of them.

entry.title: The unintended consequences of uninvited guests
entry.content:
Long Ass Day

Depression and I have been wrestling since last two weeks.

What's helped is taking my meds on time and working out.

Having a routine is important because when you're in the hole all your days blur together.

This morning I completed my run. It was 9 kms. It felt good to run so much. I don't gas out like I used to late last year.

The cut is also going great. I'm steadily losing about 1kg every week.

I guess the major reason I was depressed unconsciously was because it would have been my 5th anniversary with my ex.

To distract myself from what feels like heartache and heartbreak I train hard.

It might be a weird thing to say but if you are physically in some amount of discomfort it takes away from the thoughts ™️

My evening routine after MMA is to just curl up in a warm blanket in a cold room watching Netflix.

So when that routine gets interrupted by uninvited guests it really makes me feel like I am fighting gods hardest battles.

So now here I am, outside the comfort of my room when I am supposed to be resting and recovering, buying dinner after we have already ate for someone who came without informing us.

I don't know who started this trend of showing up without informing, but I genuinely hope that person has a bad day tomorrow.

Because the last thing I need after getting punched and kneed in the stomach a hundred times each is having to take my scooter in the night on pothole filled roads dodging gig workers doing the accident trifecta: scrolling on YouTube shorts, one hand on the handle, and no helmet.

The worst part of this whole ordeal is they drank my last diet coke. Nobody buys it in this house, but somehow everyone loves drinking it.

I know this is a bit of a rant post but it's healthier to write down and express myself as opposed to malding in my room with the aftermath.

My disappointment is immeasurable and my evening is ruined.

entry.title: Don’t Lose Your Sveltia CMS Drafts
entry.content:
Saving future me from past me.

If you’re like me and using Astro + Sveltia CMS for your website, you might want to add this script.

Last week, I lost all my changes from a draft after spending over 20 minutes writing it, and it was incredibly frustrating. Sveltia does have a restore option that appears when you reopen the page, but I find it a little finicky. I’d much rather have a warning before I accidentally close or refresh the page.

I honestly thought this was already built in.

diff --git a/src/pages/admin/index.astro b/src/pages/admin/index.astro
index 443089b8..e7f27483 100644
--- a/src/pages/admin/index.astro
+++ b/src/pages/admin/index.astro
@@ -19,5 +19,26 @@
 
       init({ config: cmsConfig });
     </script>
+
+  <script>
+    let isDirty = false;
+
+    function isInEditor() {
+      const hash = location.hash;
+      return hash.includes('/entries/') || hash.endsWith('/new');
+    }
+
+    for (const event of ['input', 'change']) {
+      document.addEventListener(event, () => {
+        if (isInEditor()) isDirty = true;
+      }, true);
+    }
+
+    window.addEventListener('hashchange', () => { isDirty = false; });

entry.title: [Blog] Birthday B̶l̶u̶e̶s̶ Purples
entry.content:
I used to have a complicated relationship with my birthday. I have spent the better part of my adulthood pretending it didn't exist. Because I used to hate being alive, I didn't want to celebrate that I was still here. I also didn't understand the social games people played with gifts, and expectations they had around their own birthdays and parties. If I didn't acknowledge mine, surely I could opt out of the concept entirely?

A good friend changed some of this a few years ago by demanding care in the form of acknowledging and celebrating their birthday, and expecting (good) gifts. Because I loved them, I obliged. Now I am in a much healthier place with my own.

What I did this year

My birthday fell on a Sunday! And the Saturday was a gfgf - so I took myself out to a good party, dressing up, looking hot, and knowing that I can show myself a good time. I went alone (didn't have the energy to make plans with friends) but immediately met 12 people i know (bangalore queer circles are MUCH bigger than they were in 2016, but they're still small enough! What can I say) and really just danced. Bodies feel so good when they do what you want.

I woke up on Sunday with a mild hangover and a craving for ramen, so I took myself to Kuuraku, did some shopping after, and came back home just in time for some dearest friends to trickle into a small hang Shru had very kindly decided to make happen at my place. We hung out, then I changed into my pajamas and went to bed at 10pm. Fantastic day, couldn't have asked for more.

How did this happen?

  1. I am finally able to be alone and take joy in my own company. I don't how to tell you how to make that happen. Maybe a decade of therapy? Somehow, when I am by myself now, I am a 29-year-old adult with a full and fascinating life, not a 5-year-old girl left to entertain herself for hours and days and weeks on end. I am not afraid to be by myself. I can take care of myself not just physically but also spiritually, emotionally. For the first time in my life, over the last year I have repeatedly chosen spending time with myself over (excellent!) company, and had a good time.
  2. I have proof that people exist and they love me. This isn't a birthday thing - it is a feeling that follows me every day, throughout the year. Birthdays in popular culture are made out to be this big production where the day is supposed to be all about you/a way for people to show you who they are to you. But that is fake! (and also capitalism). So I've learnt to slowly let go of the expectation of a big thing, and look at what I do have and revel in that. I also did get several messages wishing me and the reminder felt good :)
  3. Knowing that I didn't have to stress about plans for the day but was still going to meet friends was incredibly freeing. I am so, so grateful to Shru for making this happen. I was initially excited about throwing a big party, but I spent the whole week before (and the week after) my birthday dealing with a really intense conflict and I was not in the space to plan or engage with other people. But she created group, set up snacks and punch, and coordinated people. My home is always set up for having guests so nothing else needed to be done. Doing emotional and intellectual labour for me is always its own gift, and this one was so lovely!

I'm looking forward to the next several decades of birthdays!

entry.title: An education in the age of automation
entry.content:
We are yet again in a state of flux where a formal education is being questioned. It’s not the first time we are here, though. In a capitalistic world, education may feel unnecessary if your goal is to earn, and you will find examples of people who have skipped it entirely and are doing well.[^1]

I am not one of them.

Once upon a time, I was a young engineering grad who had just started exploring front-end design. I would download PSDs and work on new JS frameworks. I knew nothing about design. Heck, I didn’t even know you could get a degree in it. In 2011–12, a specific sequence of events led me into design school. I felt design school would teach me how to make websites and apps. Boy, was I wrong (and glad to have been).

Design school pedagogy came as a surprise to me, someone who had spent all my life studying in traditional educational institutions that had subjects, exams and fixed time periods—working like clockwork through the academic year. Design school, on the other hand, had modules, assignments and juries with a lot of time left for you to explore. The syllabus began with Foundation. You’d think that means being taught the basics. It doesn’t. There are no teachers here, just faculty. You’re expected to start doing. If you had never drawn, or painted, or done craft, it’s a rude awakening as you see people around you excelling while whatever you do seems rubbish. You could give up, thinking that it’s a dead skill, or you could recognize you aren’t good enough. This is an important choice and one which governs what you do at design school. I’ve seen folks in my batch of 14 dismiss the need to draw type by hand on an A3 on a weekend[^2] since they felt you could get the same outcome on Illustrator. But the outcome was never the intention of the assignment. It was the journey.[^3]

“Each time I sit myself down with fifteen, twenty, however many many books (or book covers), I give myself a fresh opportunity for observation and discovery. All of it fills up my creative cup. And depending on the other ingredients swirling around in this metaphorical cup on that day, I see different patterns and make different connections.”

–– Pooja Saxena

Design school education isn’t really about making your portfolio or learning tools. A good design school would never optimise for teaching you tools, but rather teach you how to approach and tackle real problems, be it system design or group work. Design school gives you the freedom to develop yourself; it gives you a few years to step away, introspect and immerse yourself in trivial pursuits or while away the hours with friends.

“You get to follow ideas, develop taste, fail, and figure out what you actually care about as a designer!”

–– Jean Chen

That brings us to the second important aspect of a design school: the people. You are going to be part of a cohort, one chosen by a panel and expected to work together and learn from each other. The people you spend your days with, and the conversations you have with them, will probably matter more than the faculty of the institution.

You will meet people and their obsessions(or witness the creation of a new one), you will learn from people about things you had no idea about (and perhaps start caring for those ideas), you will see people embark on long term projects (and maybe you will be inspired to do the same. You will find yourself staying up late arguing about an idea, or partying till daylight (or both). If I were you, I wouldn’t miss this for the world. If I had to choose again, I would choose going to design school every time. They were some of the best days of my life. Though, in hindsight, I probably should have spent a little more of that time working.

As I end the post, I acknowledge that a good design school education is a privilege that few have access to. I am conscious of my privilege, and I am writing this post to implore those of you who are currently at the threshold of such a decision to take that leap of faith. You may not end up getting a job after it, but I hope you acquire an open mind, develop great friendships and make core memories in those years. Design school changed me, and I feel it was for the better. I didn't know it would when I was taking the leap, but I am so glad that I took it.

[^1]: Header image: taken at the Bauhaus Design Museum. Taken at the Bauhaus Design Museum, Dessau.

[^2]: That’s me, hand-lettering a poster in design school.

[^3]: Reinhold Rossig, specimen sheet from lessons with Joost Schmidt, 1929. Indian ink and pencil on paper. Taken at the Bauhaus Design Museum, Dessau.

entry.title: Poor Economics
entry.content:
I picked up a cheapo duplicate copy of Poor Economics by Banerjee and Duflo, bought from a bookstore in Kochi when I went to a friend's wedding.

It feels like I understand the mechanics and economics of poverty much better now. My favourite chapter was the one about microfinance (aged well, nail on the head), and the one about poor people and their relationship to entrepreneurship.

Much of the book is explaining behaviours of the poor that are incomprehensible to people (especially WEIRD people) who haven't actually talked to or known much about poor people. some of this is backed by randomized controlled trials that won them the (economics) Nobel prize.

Examples of these behaviours:

  • When the very poor get more money or subsidies, they don't maximise calories per dollar or spend more on necessities, they'd spend on tastier calories and entertainment, and this is a very rational behaviour given their circumstances.

  • The poor would rather spend on cures and injections and expensive healthcare things, rather than cheap preventive things that require follow-ups (like immunization or micronutrient supplement/fortification).

In general, I feel like this whole RCT methodology is a narrow frame to look at the problem and selects for a certain way of doing things. Thankfully they do supplement it with ethnography and interviewing of subjects.

It's also been ~15 years since this book came out came out so a lot changed. Which also means I could do a lot of digging with my AI to "follow-up" on this book essentially. Few things that stood out to me:

  • The book focused a lot on India, Indonesia and SEA for its research generally, and not too much on Africa. Right now most extreme poverty is basically in Subsaharan Africa and war-torn countries, not so much in India and SEA generally. Unsure how much of the findings will replicate/transfer.

  • India's poverty dropped from ~27% when the book was out to something like ~5-10% (lots of debate over how much reduction, because of measuring methodology changes, etc, but no dispute that it has reduced).

  • The book deliberately champions small changes and microeconomics stuff, and leaves out macro stuff. This is good overall, because it's a lot more actionable and small changes do add up and inform policy. However, from digging up data, it seems like the macro stuff is what really has driven poverty reduction in India rather than the micro-interventions in this book. Specifically from pulling up stuff from microdata.gov.in and other such sources, it appears to me that rise in wages (due to there being more jobs and non-agricultural jobs) and more women in the workforce explains at least three quarters of the reduction. The micro stuff seems to have mattered a lot more in subsaharan Africa with respect to stuff like bednets/malaria etc. Unfortunately, since 2025, foreign aid that made this happen has basically been cut off.

  • The psych/behavioural economics explanations have aged poorly due to the replication crisis, though their research didn't rely too much on these. It was used more to support the explanation for their findings.

  • UPI and cheap mobile money transfers is a thing now, which it wasn't then. So a lot of intervention options have opened due to being able to send money at scale, and "is this better than just wiring in some cash" is a default baseline to measure any kind of policy intervention against.

  • The worst-aged parts are the enthusiasm for Aadhar (always referred to as ~"Nilekani's ID project"). It was not even launched yet, and the authors were hopeful that this would reduce subsidy theft. Extremely strange, given the authors avoid speculation and only speak based on data for just about everything else. Leaving aside all the privacy/surveillance stuff, I looked at whether it actually reduced subsidy theft, and the answer is "kind of." The thing is, it isn't clear that this reduced theft more than what any other normal kind of system of record/non-biometric digital verification might have, and the cost of operationalising Aadhar has been very high.

entry.title: Customizing Miniflux: Sorting by Signal
entry.content:
I have been using Miniflux as my feed reader for a couple of years now. As mentioned in a previous note, I have customized it to add custom sorting for articles. In the last note I added sorting by similarity. In this note, I add another method to it: sorting by signal.

This post was originally published on abhinavsarkar.net.

This post is a part of the series: Customizing Miniflux.

  1. Making a Two-Pane Reader
  2. Addding Custom Sorting
  3. Sorting by Similarity
  4. Sorting by Signal 👈

As scores of new articles keep coming into my feed reader every day, I found myself looking for a new way to find the actually interesting ones. So, I invented it! This quality of interest, which I have dubbed Signal, is decided by two factors:

  1. Age of the article: I often find myself skip reading articles that seem interesting at a glance, but are too long to read immediately. Such articles keep getting older and get lost in my feed. So I consider older articles to be more interesting than newer ones. Also because, newness is the default sorting, and I read most new articles anyway. I want to find the old gems that are there in my feed, but I’ve forgotten about. So, older articles are scored more.
  2. Number of articles from a domain: If a website publishes articles rarely, they are most likely to be interesting, compared to a website that puts out many articles every week. So fewer the number of articles from a domain, higher it should be scored1.

I put them together in this scoring formula:

\[ \text{Score} = \frac{\text{Oldest Age}}{\text{Article Count}^{\alpha}} \times \left(1 + \frac{\text{Article Age}}{\text{Oldest Age}} \right) \]

where \(Oldest Age\) and \(Article Count\) are per domain.

This formula scores older articles from domains with fewest articles higher. The second part of the formula avoids clumping all articles from same domain together. The \(\alpha\) parameter is used to control how much we favour article age over article count. For \(\alpha = 1\), domains with high article counts are penalized heavily, and for \(\alpha = 0\), there is no penalty for having multiple articles per domain, only article ages matter.

Here is the custom JavaScript for sorting by Signal: 
function sortEntriesBySignal(entries) {
  const now = Date.now();
  const domainStats = {};

  let entryData = [];
  for (const entry of entries) {
    const domain = entryUrl(entry).split("/")[0].replace(/^www\./, "");
    const ageHours = Math.max(
      now - new Date(entryTime(entry)).getTime() / 3600000,
      0.1,
    );
    if (!domainStats[domain]) {
      domainStats[domain] = { count: 0, oldestAge: 0 };
    }
    domainStats[domain].count++;
    if (ageHours > domainStats[domain].oldestAge) {
      domainStats[domain].oldestAge = ageHours;
    }
    entryData.push({ entry: entry, domain: domain, age: ageHours });
  }

  const ALPHA = 0.8;
  for (const data of entryData) {
    const stats = domainStats[data.domain];
    const baseScore = stats.oldestAge / Math.pow(stats.count, ALPHA);
    const score = baseScore * (1 + data.age / stats.oldestAge);
    data["score"] = score;
  }

  return entryData
    .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score)
    .map((data) => data.entry);
}

You can see the full code with all the sorting methods here.

That’s it! This works very well for me, and I hope this helps someone else too.

If you have any questions or comments, please leave a comment below. If you liked this post, please share it. Thanks for reading!

  1. I group the articles by domain instead of feed because many of my feeds contain articles from multiple domains, such as my read-later feed and feeds of the blogrolls I subscribe to.↩︎
