entry.title: IndiaFOSS 2026
entry.content:
Dumping the memories before I forget them.

This was my first time attending IndiaFOSS. It’s an annual conference held by FOSS United which tries to cover a variety of topics and bring together people of all age groups and diversity ;) There should be more such events!

The 2026 edition took place on 26th and 27th of September at NIMHANS Convention Center and it was amazing! I had a blast talking to people, attending talks, and all the booths — the energy was unmatched 🔥

Before attending the event, I was going through their schedule to select the talks I was interested in. The community had built a dating-app style website for selecting your talks (thanks to Amogh for telling us) 😆 Honestly, a great idea. Let’s move on to the actual funsies now :D

📝 Note: All the talk recordings are available on the FOSS United YouTube channel.

#First Day

I left quite early in the morning with Harsh and Fenil. We reached well before the Welcome Note. After inhaling the breakfast and coffee, Fenil and I headed towards Hall 3 which was designated for the Open Hardware devroom while Harsh went to the Documentation & Technical Writing one.

I generally like working with Hardware and Software, so I was leaning towards this one and I loved all the talks! The halls were fully packed! Let’s take a look at each of them:

#Build your own Open source keyboard with ZMK/QMK

As a person who has spent A LOT on Keyboards, this was amazing. More so because the guy worked at Mecha and I’ve been following them for quite some time. I really like their product and the whole process/documentation around it ;) If you don’t, go check it out!

I did not know about ZMK and how it’s designed as a Wireless first firmware, this is so cool!

#CNC4Everyone - How we built a CNC machine for every classroom, college and makerspace

I expected a larger CNC machine when I first saw their presentation, but it was quite compact and was for a different set of people. I am all in for making such things that can be put in classrooms. I still remember back then we had a 3D printer in my school when it was not so easily available at all! They also used 3D printers for many parts ;)

There was this quote that was mentioned: “China can fill a stadium with CNC operators and we won’t fill a room” — this is why we need easier accessibility to hobby electronics, 3D printers, etc.

#My zero-to-hero journey deploying a fiber-optic and wireless community mesh

This was the talk I was most interested in as a networking nerd! As Fenil likes to call it, the guy had peak FAFO (Fuck Around, Find Out) energy. Kiran talked about how he, along with a few friends, pooled in to buy a farmland 100kms away from the city and wanted to set up WiFi there.

He got an uplink from BSNL, bought 1km (yes, that much) of fiber-optic cable and had to call a lineman in for Fusion Splicing (and are now setting up weather stations???). Mad respect 🫡

There wasn’t much time for him to go into network details, but man, I wish I could hear more! I spent around 2 hours just talking to him outside in the second half and it was so worth it! More on this later :P

#Building Open Source Music Hardware in India

Another guy with a similar energy but in the music industry. He dropped some banger lines: “Being broke is the mother of invention” and “The thing with doing anything is that you really just have to do it.” I’ve always been fascinated with music hardware like MIDI Controllers.

He talked about building the first prototype in just 2000 INR and how the design improved over time. He also mentioned that building the same thing again and again is not fun when you have to sell it, so he told people to just DIY 😆

I also love that he gave back to the community, especially around where to buy parts since that’s a huge pain in India :)

#Minnow: An Open Platform for Ground Swarm Robotics

The idea of Swarm robotics is quite cool. I’ve worked with autonomous robots back in school with things like 1Sheeld (RIP) and Arduino. It was a lot of fun, I miss those days 🥲

He talks about building a 100x cheaper alternative to the TurtleBot, which is fascinating! He wants people to use Minnow as a base to build other things 🔥 I am all in for such projects!

This concludes the first half of the day and the next devroom happening here was the Compilers, Programming languages and Systems. I attended the first talk about Semantic Quantization in KV Cache Eviction which went completely over my head 🫠

I decided to leave the hall for a BoF (Birds of a Feather) about Homelab and Self Hosting which is right in my alley! This is an informal gathering which happens every year at IndiaFOSS where people talk about what has changed in their homelab since the last year, and it was fun hearing people talk. I also yapped about my setup with people and a few stuck with me for a while, where we were discussing our bad financial decisions ranging from running an RTX GPU 24x7 to buying a Dell PowerEdge server.

Afterwards, I went to the workstation set up by Kiran where he wanted people to come and help build the first weather station. I talked to him about various things that I found interesting, like how he’s using LoRa for broadcasting weather data, the amount of hardware he has, and how it all started — just too many things! It’s like discovering a goldmine 🪎 I learned some cool things about him:

  • He built his own 350x350mm 3D printer, and that too a VORON!!!
  • He started all this just 2 years ago (that’s crazy to me)
  • He’s planning to open a Makerspace eventually,

I wish he documented all these FAFO projects somewhere because this is exactly what I want to read! It reminds me of Jeff Geerling ;) Here’s a picture of me drilling holes in a metal sheet beside him:

After roaming around at a few booths with Fenil, we went out with people from FP India, Rust India, and PyCon India :P The whole mixed bag and it was quite fun getting to know people, plus some of them already knew me from reading my blogs 🫶

#Second Day

On the second day, we got a bit late but arrived just in time for breakfast :P After which, we headed to the Security devroom which was again in Hall 3!

#Reverse Engineering the PAN QR Code

It’s funny how bad the government security implementations are and how they claim something which it isn’t. The reverse engineering part was quite interesting and how he was able to build an open-source scanner for the thing which the government says is closed source.

He also mentioned that they don’t publish the PAN spec anywhere unlike Aadhaar 🙃 (our data is public anyway but oh well)

#When NO_PROXY Lies: Finding an IPv4-Mapped IPv6 Patch Bypass in Axios

Every day I am reminded that people don’t wanna use IPv6, but then there’s this RCA where networking libraries relied on string matching rather than identity matching for addresses.

Networking is hard.

#Extracting AES Keys from Embedded Devices Using Open Source Hardware

This was super interesting and a very unique approach which I’ve never seen before. They showcased how they were able to extract each bit of an AES encryption key by passing in random plaintext and connecting a ChipWhisperer to pull out a power graph with an oscilloscope and correlate it with their “synthetic one”.

This needs quite an ideal scenario though, since you need to know on what pin exactly the encryption is happening. This will be much harder on modern chips, say something like TPM.

#The Art of Userspace Sandboxing on Linux

This talk was quite theoretical with no demos which is not a bad thing. The content was quite good and explained mostly everything one needs to know about basic Sandboxing.

I wish he added AI agents with Sandboxing as an example which would’ve been quite relevant and interesting for people ;)

#Keeping an Eye on your Eye: Disassembling and Reassembling Smart Camera Hardware to breach YOUR Security

This talk was the peak of the event, absolutely chaotic. They set up a live soldering station 😭 in the middle of the stage and everything that could go wrong, went wrong. The laptop crashed in between while showcasing, the HDMI input kept losing its signal, and the IC on the PCB which he was trying to remove got burnt. The last thing remaining was to trigger the fire alarm ☠️

It was so random but I absolutely loved this. The guy was a sport, he made the most out of it 😆 Unfortunately, they couldn’t present the firmware reverse engineering part completely, but I understood the gist of it.

#Hacking India’s Largest Exam System

It’s incredible how incompetent the people at CBSE and CERT-IN are at taking responsibility :) They tried to get away from it by changing CNAME records 😭 even Claude could do a better job… Overall, a pretty good job by Nisarga and at such a young age 🫡 It was so funny looking at all the things CBSE tried and failed.

After the security devroom, we decided to attend this panel discussion around future of FOSS, SWE and Technical Education. It was about LLMs as expected and people on the panel just saying that “Our company does not do this or that” isn’t really helpful for anyone. This is a privileged take that you aren’t using LLMs as you’re supposed to just because you can.

People working in corporate have to choose between using LLMs or unemployment, I bet you can differentiate between those. We left for lunch in the middle since this wasn’t really adding any value to our time.

In the second half, we went booth hopping and spent some time talking with Dev from Gooey.AI team and Anoop from Bruno. We then headed for the Communi-Con which is like a mini-conf with lightning talks that the community voted on!

All the talks were quite fun, ranging from postmarketOS, self hosting on a phone, Elixir (with some philosophy), hating on JavaScript (as intended), etc. They also gave us a live voting website where we could decide if the person stays on stage or not after 5 minutes, which was fun xD

#Network Setup at the Venue by COSH

This was a talk I accidentally ended up in and was immediately interested in! The WiFi range was quite good in each corner and they used the Dot1X protocol for authentication!

I also looked at their router earlier in the day, wondering what they were using, so this was perfect! They did a very good job 🎉

#IndiaFOSS 2027 by Shree

  • 20+ devrooms: This will be super nice, much more topics to cover!
  • Few changes to Main Track:
    • Renamed to General Track
    • Shrinking it down: It had the largest hall and was half empty most of the time while people did not have seats to sit in other Devrooms (this is a welcome change)
    • Cheaper tickets for students and an RSVP system

After the event, I ended up going out again with Harsh, Fenil, the FP and Rust India group. It was a nice outing :)

#Booths

During the event, I went around a lot of booths and people had put so much time and care into each one of them! Everyone was super nice and had a lot of different things going on, diversity is good!

  • Data for India had a nice guessing game for different statistics where we failed on 2/3 :P I went here to also say hi to Arpit (fellow IWC member)
  • There was also a booth of Tangled. I’ve already used their platform before and I really like it (plus they use Nix). The new features which they showcased in their Communi-Con talk were great!
  • Paper Crane Labs had a nice booth with 3D printers and you could also solve a puzzle (I couldn’t)
  • I loved the booth of DiagramChasing and their illustrations are super nice to look at!
  • There was an OSM booth, always nice to see :) I want to join their mapping events someday!
  • There was a Debian booth where they kept a Busy Bar! I love that little piece of hardware and now I’m tempted to buy it again 😭

I somehow missed the Bengawalk booth :(

#Closing Notes

Some more things that I liked:

  • There was a lot of niche hardware like Meshtastic devices for one!
  • We kept bumping into IndieWebClub folks!
  • I really like the idea of Communi-Con, more of this!
  • The T-Shirt design 👕
  • A lot of stickers!
  • The food 🥗

And finally, a photo of me with Fenil and Harsh at the event:

Tanvi trying to photobomb us, better luck next time 😆

Before leaving, check out posts from fellow IndieWebClub members:

  • https://adithyanair.com/blog/indiafoss-2026/
  • https://blog.skaup.co/indiafoss-2026.html
  • https://fknil.com/blog/india-foss-2026/
  • https://kaustubh.page/posts/reflections-from-indiafoss-2026/

I had a lot of fun, see y’all next year 🕊️

entry.title: My experience at IndiaFOSS 2026
entry.content:
I’ve been making more of an effort this year to show up to meetups and events happening in the area so I eagerly looking forward to IndiaFOSS 2026. A lot of my friends over at the IndieWebClub were also planning to visit so there was going to be no lack of familiar faces, and hopefully some new ones too 😄

Day 1

Fenil, Yash, and I had decided to leave together bright and early so Fenil biked down to our place and we took a cab together. We made it well in time for breakfast and the welcome keynote, after which we split up with Fenil and Yash heading to the Open Hardware devroom while I headed over to the Documentation & Technical Writing devroom.

The quality of the talks was quite high, and while AI inevitably comes up when talking about documentation; it was refreshing to see Ganesh Devgan from Bruno reaffirm that good documentation will continue to be written for humans.

Vinamra Harkar presented a very engaging talk about discovering the National Informatics Center’s newsletter named Informatics that has been running since July 1992, and his journey of converting this stack of PDFs into an indexed, searchable resource spanning 30+ years. I browsed through some of the older issues, and there are some fascinating stories there about the technological advances being made at country-scale to bring up India’s digital capabilities as the Internet started gaining ground. It’s almost like a portal to a time we can scarcely imagine, where computers were a rarity and not something that is now in most people’s pockets.

I decided to ditch the documentation devroom for a bit to roam around the booths and find some friends. After stuffing my pockets with stickers, I joined Yash and Fenil in the Open Hardware devroom right in time for Balu Babu’s talk about Minnow, a swarm robotics project he has been working on and off since college. With an overarching goal of capping the per-unit pricing of the device around the 3000 INR mark, he walked us through the tradeoffs he’s made and how the software architecture has evolved to bring this ambitious goal closer to reality.

Next up was Syed Ali walking us through the journey of building Open Source Music Hardware in India. His initial foray was modest, a desire for a cheaper alternative to a prohibitively expensive MIDI controller that he was confident was simple enough electronically to be made for cheap. We walked through his journey of discovering Open Hardware, building his first controller and eventually selling it, and then making a side hustle out of it. He shared his tier lists for vendors to buy parts from, and some more of the custom gear he had since built.

It was time for lunch now, where we saw Tanvi and Ankur and chatted for a bit. After the meal we split up again, Yash and Fenil went to the Compilers, Programming Languages & Systems devroom while I headed to the AOSP devroom with Amogh.

My main objective was to meet Amit Pundir, who was one of the first people to ever invite me to a conference, all the way back in 2018 and we’ve kept in touch since. The devroom had some interesting talks but most people very obviously used Claude to generate their slides, and the telltale signs of “Claudish”1 were rather annoying to read through. I grumbled about it on Mastodon and Amit responded saying he’ll be passing the feedback along and try to keep a higher quality gate moving forward. I’m going to try and get involved with the local FOSS United chapter, and hopefully help out with CFP review for next year’s iteration of the AOSP devroom to improve on this.

Harsh Shandilya@msfjarvis@fantastic.earth

After Amit's opening keynote and lightning talk, almost every session I've seen in the AOSP devroom has had blatantly Claude generated slides. Very disappointing that people continue to delegate prose to LLMs when they're knowledgeable enough about the topic at hand to do it themselves.

#IndiaFOSS

26 Sept 2026, 10:53View original post ↗

That said, the talks themselves were mostly quite enjoyable and I learned a lot. Karthikeyan’s talk about porting AOSP to the Allwinner Sunxi platform dove deep into the quirks of the Sunxi SoCs and how they got different components to work on these chips and finally get to AOSP. It was pretty interesting to learn how displays work under the hood, from the Android internals all the way to the kernel drivers.

After the devroom Amogh and I went back to sticker collection, and met a bunch of friends. Amogh’s quite popular over here! Though I imagine being at a debConf and running the FOSS Mumbai event will do that 😄

We reunited with Yash and Fenil to yap for a bit, after which they left for a cafe in Jayanagar with some of Fenil’s friends from the FP/Rust circles, and Amogh and I headed back home.

Day 2

I woke up feeling quite tired so I decided to skip most of the day 2 event, and only went for the off-track Communi-Con event. We had dinner plans for that day so the timing was also going to work out for me. I had voted on the proposals on day 1, and was pleased to find most of my picks had indeed won out and got selected. There were a total of 7 lightning talks but I’ll only highlight a few here.

The FOSS United volunteer team that had taken on the task of having visitor Wi-Fi available for the first time in IndiaFOSS history went through their physical network architecture, and the software stack behind it. They had laid out nearly 4 kilometers of cabling across 2 floors to provide (in my experience) reliable connectivity to all attendees. It was quite impressive, and I hope the tear down was less grueling than installing all of it!

Kailash Nadh had an incendiary talk titled “Say no to JS React garbage” about his story of constantly fighting JS framework churn working on listmonk and eventually choosing to build his own NodeJS-free component library called Oat and deleting thousands of line of JavaScript in listmonk while regaining control of his frontend stack. I have been using Oat for my personal web apps since the beginning of this year and share all his frustrations and how relieving it is to simply rely on the platform than invent abstractions on top.

Shree Kumar presented some bold ideas on what he thinks IndiaFOSS 2027 needs to evolve into to achieve its goal of unifying FOSS in India. More devrooms, bigger venues, more student tickets were only the start of what he has in mind. Excitedly waiting to see if the new governing board members share his vision!

Communi-con was probably the most fun part of the event, and I hope it makes a comeback next year.

After the talks we did another round on the proverbial hallway track, then headed out with some of Fenil’s friends to The Bloom cafe for some coffee/food/yapping. My social battery had started to run out by then so I mostly spent that time finishing up my weeknote that I had mercifully pre-written most of on Friday expecting to not be home to publish it.

All things considered, IndiaFOSS was extremely fun if exhausting and I would like to visit more FOSS United events in the future! Also check out Fenil’s blog about his IndiaFOSS experience, who decidedly had a more fun time :D

  1. Claudish is the dense, jargon-heavy register Claude and similar coding agents default to — compressed metaphors, invented compound nouns, and objects doing action verbs. ↩

entry.title: To, My College Juniors
entry.content:
Hello hello! How are ya? ¶

A lot of you guys have been getting in touch with me recently. Placements have been a pain, haven’t they? I remember feeling that way. You might also believe that you guys have it worse than our batch, and I don’t disagree with that either. ¶

My final semester of college was pretty far from sunshine and rainbows, and I remember feeling at the time that it won’t get any better. I remember the exhaustion and the frustration, the late nights preparing and the early mornings revising. It felt like the world was on my shoulders. ¶

I want to share a bit about how that burden felt for me and my friends, with the hope that you find some part of yourself in it. Through all of the storytelling, I just want to let you know that I feel ya. ¶

I think the pressure for me began particularly at the end of 3rd Year. There had been many companies dropping in throughout 6th Semester, and I’d convinced myself that I would receive an internship in atleast one of them. But the NeoPAT app slowly started showing less entries, as the rejection emails and ghosting piled up. ¶

By the time I could worry about it I had to prepare for my finals, and the only time I could sit and think about it was on the flight back home. ¶

A lot of my friends had internships, some of them stretching into their 7th Semester with the promise of conversion. There were also people who had set their eyes on higher education, and were already preparing to give the exams and fill the applications. Everyone seemed to be moving smoothly except me. ¶

I was still known in college as a Former President of CodeX, and a Chapter Lead of Null-OWASP. The guy that did a lot of big software things. So I also remember feeling shame when I wasn’t able to live up to that “reputation” I was known for. But that’s a story for another day. ¶

I spent a good while at home just moping. The mood shifted from “they didn’t really deserve me” to “I really need to lock in now” to “should I forget about all this and give CAT instead?” and back again. ¶

I had my moments where I was productive, eventually. I worked with a tech consultancy for some time and built a project for them. I worked with another consultancy for a one-time website. I caught up with LinkedIn project posts so that my profile still seemed active, and I also thankfully had an internship I had done during 3rd Year1 that I could present as summer work. ¶

None of it was big or permanent, but I had already accepted that I would have to give my all during the Final Year to actually get placed somewhere. I’m glad that my parents were supportive throughout this, and even let me entertain the idea of giving CAT completely2. ¶

I spent the rest of my vacation meeting up with friends and spending time with family, because there would be less time for all that in the months to come. ¶

The classes were smaller and emptier in the Final Year; a lot of students had left for an internship in their 7th Semester instead of starting in the 8th. Attendance wasn’t taken that seriously anymore, probably because the professors understood that our priorities were different now. ¶

I’d never been one to pay attention in class, and would get away with studying right before the exam to learn everything. So before long, I was taking advantage of the lax schedule to spend more and more time doing my own thing. The teachers probably noticed, but decided not to say anything. ¶

I’d always had roommates throughout being in hostel. They were different every year, and I was lucky enough that all of them were lovely; I say that because I’ve heard accounts from other friends about some bad, bad roommates. I was even lucky enough that I could choose3 my roommate in 3rd Year, and got a double room with one of my closest friends. ¶

In 4th Year though, pretty much anyone I was close to had either joined somewhere for an internship or was already paired up with someone else. I didn’t want the risk of getting a bad roommate assigned, so I decided (with much privilege) to instead go for a single room. Ironically, that might be where my loneliness began. ¶

You see, a roommate is always there. There’s always another human presence in the room, doing something of their own and going about their own life. There’s liveliness in the room even when you’re not being lively. ¶

Also, roommates usually go through the same thing that you are, at the same time as you. All students have assignments due during the same week, and have exams in the same time period. They all begin to stay up late preparing, become delirious, and crash out about exams and professors roughly around the same time. They remind you that there are other people going through the same thing as you. ¶

In a single room though, time seems to move a lot slower. It only moves when you move. There isn’t a gauge for when you’re being slow, or even when you’re being productive. It is a lot more alone, and that feeling slowly exhausted me; as if I was continuously wading through mud, watching every step, and yet not really sure where I was going. ¶

I continued on with assessments and interviews with that feeling in the back of my mind. NeoPAT would send a notification, I would register, show up on the day of the assessment, and then wait. There would almost never be a notification that you weren’t taken forward; instead, you would just slowly learn that the people who were selected were contacted separately. It was a little more hurtful when received like that. ¶

I soon learned to hate DSA. God, I hated DSA. It was a pathetic excuse for companies to not put effort into crafting individual questions, and to grade students on an absolute scale of 0 to 100. They took away your Internet privileges in an age where almost all software is written for the Internet, with the hope that you would somehow remember every single function in your language of choice4. ¶

Editor’s Note: The rest of the above paragraph has been cut short to stay on topic. There were many words involved that would make even sailors fluster. If you want the full version, ask the author out for chai.

But anyway, after a long and tiring routine of seeing the same graphs and matrix questions and never fully solving them5, I saw hope when a certain company did the whole thing differently. Let’s call them… HydroWinds. ¶

HydroWinds was special. They had coding challenges that didn’t put you in a box, and needed you to explore solutions to actually succeed. They wanted you to use specific languages, but with full access to the documentation (to see how quickly you can learn a new language and apply it). I could do it all, and before long I was waiting for the shortlist for the final interview. ¶

We received the shortlist. At 4PM on Friday. The interview was at 10AM on the next day, at the main campus in Udupi. Over 400 kilometers away. ¶

The next 36 hours were the most chaotic of my life. ¶

A WhatsApp group was made with all the finalists from Bengaluru. Multiple bus portals were checked and tickets were booked just before they sold out. I didn’t have formal shoes, so my uncle bought them and brought them to the hostel while I packed my bag for the next two nights. All of this while coordinating the hostel outpass ourselves. ¶

We would have to leave for our bus past our 10PM curfew, and so needed to get an approval from the Chief Student Officer (with zero assistance from the Placement Committee) so we can actually reach for our interviews in time. Somehow after juggling it all, we were standing on a noisy bus stop at 11PM waiting for our GreenLine bus to arrive. ¶

The ride was bumpy. I don’t believe any of us actually got any sleep. At one point while lying down, the bus jumped and my whole body was in the air, right before I crashed down and hit my head hard enough that I couldn’t sleep again. ¶

We arrive at the destination an hour later than the scheduled time. We travel from the bus stop to the hostel ourselves, without being provided any directions. Apparently the logistics weren’t taken care of beforehand, so we spent another 30 minutes making payments and receiving keys to our rooms one-by-one. ¶

We somehow enter our rooms at around 9AM and start getting ready to reach the Placement Building by 10. Ah, finally, just enough time to catch our breath—- ¶

An unknown number calls one of the interviewees: ¶

“Where are you all?! You were supposed to reach the Placement Hall by 7.30AM! If you don’t reach in the next 30 minutes, we will remove you from the process.”

After all our luck so far, we didn’t question why we needed to be there at 7.30 when the email said 10. We just got ready and ran. When we arrived at the building, the placement representative looked at us dubiously. “Why did you guys rush? The interviews won’t start for another hour, you could’ve taken your time.” ¶

We just sat down and caught our breath. ¶

The interviews began shortly afterward. We went through our material and prepared our documents. Earlier, when we had entered the Hall, the students from main campus sitting inside had asked us if we’re from MIT Bengaluru. When we affirmed, they snickered at us; like a scene out of a teenage high-school drama. I’m glad they did though, because the spite kept me going. ¶

I… had a lot of expectations from this interview. This was the farthest I’d ever gotten in the placement process. The tests seemed as if they were made for me, as if they understood how my brain worked. I really wanted to get through. I really wanted to stop going through placements. ¶

Right before my turn, someone mentioned a concept from object-oriented programming. I didn’t remember it, so I franctically tried to look it up and memorize it right as my name was called. ¶

I entered the room, sat down, and faced the interviewer. We greeted each other. And the question that left his mouth was not about object-oriented programming. ¶

The names for the second round of interviews were called out, and they didn’t include mine. I went out of the Hall, sat on the stairs, and called my mom. I couldn’t remember the last time I’d cried before that, but tears streamed down my face as I tried to tell my mother that I did everything I could and it wasn’t enough. “But I gave my best, mamma,” I said to her. ¶

Booking the bus ride back and re-packing was a blur. The two students who were selected were both from MIT Bengaluru, so I remember having a “Ha!” moment. One of the two students was also Raghav, a close friend, which made me even happier. But I was still empty as we went out for dinner to celebrate and met up with some friends from Manipal. ¶

Soon, I was on the way back to college while bumping up and down in the bus. I didn’t even try to sleep this time. ¶

The normalcy after reaching back made the HydroWinds process seem like a fever dream. The classes continued on, NeoPAT kept sending in notifications, and I kept giving assessments. People would ask from time to time about “what happened after you went to Manipal”, and I would try to tell them with a smile that I didn’t get it. ¶

Looking back, I felt a lot calmer after the main campus interview. I think it came from the bus ride back, when I was lying awake and realized that —- other than the two people who converted —- there were eight others travelling with me back to the college, “without success”. ¶

This feeling later extended towards other people in college. I remembered my friends who went for a 7th Semester internship; how they wished they were in college with friends, and how they felt like they were missing out on it all. I remembered the people studying for higher education, and how they felt —- with the constantly changing policies and politics —- that they were betting their future on a gamble. I remembered the girl I liked; how the college rejoiced in her placement into Big Tech, but how she constantly felt like she had to prove her worth there and gave away more and more of her personal time to work. ¶

There were people who had hardships after their placement too. People who received “Internship + Conversion”, but were blatantly fired during their internship and could do nothing about it6. Some of them ended up pursuing higher education. Some were even left stranded after the whole process, and are now sitting at home applying under pressure. Their lives have been left desolated, but the statistic shown to the next batch will not include them. ¶

I think I was floating on my own personal cloud of “oh woe is me” before, which dissolved and gave way to the understanding that everyone is here. Preparing, practicing, struggling, and feeling let down together. Some have it worse than others, some have it the worst of all, but they’re all in the same room, the same campus. They’re all reaching for the same thing in a way; some form of freedom or escape, whether it is through a high package or an Ivy League college or even just graduating successfully. They’re all looking for the process to end. ¶

This, thanks to its similarity to The Roommate Effect™, made me feel better. ¶

The day I got into BigBasket arrived unexpectedly. ¶

I’d given the assessment, just like for any other company. I’d received the shortlist and seen my name in the final interview list. I remember nodding grimly at the email, as if acknowledging an enemy I was about to fight. ¶

About 30 minutes before the interview, I decided to choose violence it would be better to trim my beard and look clean-shaven and all. I started trimming my beard and the trimmer died halfway. I was left with half a moustache and half a beard. I just giggled maniacally and sat down to join the meeting. ¶

The interviewer asked some questions from my resume, and then dropped in a DSA problem for me. I did the whole flow of explaining my process as I think and write code. I was stuck for a bit and told the interviewer I’m having trouble getting further. He told me it’s alright and that I was pretty close, gave me the rest of the solution, and then ended the interview. I just sighed and assumed it won’t go anywhere. ¶

Aaand then I received an email next week that I’d gotten the internship. ¶

Friends circled me and congratulated me. I was one of the last to receive an offer, so I’m sure some people were also relieved. Calls came in as the news spread across the extended family. The relief hadn’t really sunk in, but every well-wish was like a hammer striking “BRO YOU DID IT” into my heart. ¶

By the end of the day, I was grinning. ¶

I go to an office now. A corporate job where I carry my ID card and punch my attendance in the morning. I create Jira tickets and fill in my OKR’s. I go back home at the end of the day and have some time to myself. I get to meet my friends on the weekends who’re in Bengaluru, and we hang out together. ¶

There’s no college assignments now, and no roommates either. I’m not surrounded by a lively hostel campus or bound by a curfew. It’s a completely new place, a new leaf, whatever you want to call it. A new chapter maybe. That sounds about right. ¶

When you call me, my junior, and tell me about all the things that trouble you, it reminds me of all the times I mentioned above. I recall my own attempts and failings, my struggles and my ideas that never saw completion. I hear you completely and feel your sorrow a little too, but the best I can tell you from the other end of the process is that it will get better. Even for people from my batch struggling right now, I have no doubt they’ll find their place and comfort. Everyone eventually reaches where they want to. That’s what I believe. ¶

Oh also, never forget that your peers are experiencing the same thing as you. I say this because of some of the college happenings I’ve heard recently. It’s all very annoying to go through, but remember that you have power in numbers. Document your communication publicly, and come together for things that trouble all of you commonly. That’s the most I can say, since my degree hangs in the balance of it all too. :P ¶

Now go off. You have much succeeding to do. It’s all waiting for you. ¶

Footnotes

Footnotes

  1. I’d worked on the “Accreditation and Reporting System” under the Application Development Cell, MIT-BLR, with eight other students and some faculty. The Cell eventually went on hiatus I think, but one of the incentives we received for completing the 6-month project was an Internship Certificate from the college. ↩

  2. I ultimately decided not to go ahead with an MBA at the time, after a complete Pros/Cons comparison between CAT and a job. I realized that I just want to build things right now, not spend another two years studying theory. ↩

  3. For those unaware (or in case this has changed), our room allotment was done on the basis of academic merit. You could put in a name for someone you want as a roommate, and if your CGPA was high enough (and ofcourse, if the other person also preferred you) then you could get the same room allotted. Satyajit always had a high CGPA, I just had to catch up to him. :) ↩

  4. Sometimes not even your language of choice, actually. There were plenty of assessments that just hoped you would know C or Java or even HASKELL, but choosing your own language was too much. ↩

  5. Because, apart from hating DSA, I also never fully sat down to practice it. I think my number of Leetcode questions solved is in low double digits as of writing. This is because I have been very rigid when it comes to doing something I think is stupid. I was the same when I was giving JEE and had to prepare Physics/Chemistry/Mathematics to literally just study Computer Science. ↩

  6. Our college has a policy that students that have secured any full-time offer, with or without internship, can no longer sit for placements afterward. So these people that were promised a full-time job (and didn’t get it) were no longer supported by the college. ↩

entry.title: How Do We Get More Microgrants in India?
entry.content:
I gathered a group of folks and did the BOF session at IndiaFOSS/2026. The idea behind the BoF session wasn’t to present anything, but to solicit ideas and provocations to improve the micro-granting scene in India. There is a real need of microgrants in India. i.e., we do have big-scale grant givers and receivers, but we have very few grant givers in the range of, say, INR 50K.

My idea is how to have more such grants. What might be stopping them, especially if they want to? The discussion was informal, like all BoFs. I made small notes. But here are the takeaways from the discussion.

  1. A starter pack or playbook for new micro grant-givers, covering the problems I ran into, not just the process I settled on. The amount of work it takes, taxes, and legal questions are what worry people most. This was the biggest ask, and I think I can work on it.
  2. A 10th-year report: an optional, light email to past recipients, then a publication of short updates, blurbs, or photos to encourage others. I don’t ask folks for updates, but a lot of them do update me anyway. Folks think some grant makers are especially encouraged by the effect. So this kind of report would encourage them. I am considering this.
  3. Grants on specific themes and sponsors backing a theme, as FOSSUnited did. But in general, there could be theme-specific grant makers, and how do we make it possible for them?
  4. Publish unfunded proposals so others can support them, and use the email list actively. I am trying this; there is more to do.

Other similar funds that came up during the discussion were Helium Grants,  Escape Velocity Grants,  Sudha Mahesh Grants, and Bellare Grants; most of them are covered in this wiki.

If you think there are other ways to encourage more small grant makers to come forward and make grants. Do share them.

entry.title: Why explore our Moon
entry.content:
Many people think that the Moon is just a gray ball of rock in our sky. Surprisingly, many scientists seem to share this notion. I once had a physicist tell me the Moon is scientifically boring. That couldn’t be farther from the truth. So I wrote this article to summarize the immense scientific and exploratory value of Earth’s cosmic companion.

Firstly, consider that the bootprints of Apollo astronauts who walked on the Moon are still there, and can be seen from orbit. Since the Moon lacks an Earth-like atmosphere or running water, its surface stays virtually unchanged for years. This makes our Moon a geological time capsule, including for events Earth forgets.

During the early Solar System roughly 4 billion years ago, asteroids and comets bombarded planets and their moons at a vigorous pace. Most craters formed from such impacts on Earth are no longer visible due to erosion by wind and water or submersion. But the Moon being void of such weathering processes has preserved most of its craters in roughly the original conditions for millions and millions of years. Scientists use the Moon as an age reference to determine how old or young features on other worlds are, such as on Mars, Mercury, and moons across the Solar System. Scientists think the incoming asteroids and/or comets brought water and organics to our planet. The Moon being closer to Earth that it is today also caused larger tides, potentially facilitating mixing of key ingredients for life. Both of these factors possibly helped create of catalyze the first lifeforms. By studying the still-intact craters on the Moon from around 3.5 to 4.3 billion years ago, scientists understand what really happened during this period of our Solar System’s history, especially in Earth’s vicinity, making it a critical piece of our origin story.

Unlike Earth and Venus, the Moon lacks significant tectonic activity too—though Moonquakes do occur in smaller intensities. There are no continental plates on the Moon. As a result, our Moon’s internal structure is well preserved since its formation about 4.5 billion years ago. This means by studying the Moon’s terrain tied to interior processes, scientists found an opportunity to understand how insides of planets at large form at first. Whether its planets in our Solar System or those lying elsewhere in the Universe, the baseline physics of planetary interiors we can gauge from our Moon applies everywhere. Studying lunar mountains offer scientists a peak (pun intended) into the lunar interior, as do the Moon’s darker regions, which are solidified lava plains from the time of active volcanism on Luna. Several places on the Moon’s farside offer unique opportunities to study the lunar mantle in particular, something we’re yet to sufficiently study.

Exploring our Moon also has technological value. Luna’s proximity to Earth makes it a great testbed of technologies required for deep space exploration, including for the ambition to land humans on Mars. For example, scientists and engineers study our Moon and its environment to understand how solar radiation, high energy cosmic rays, and micrometeorite bombardment can affect astronauts living in deep space for long periods, including on Mars missions. In this century, a finding has made the Moon hold potential economic value as well. India and the US co-discovered water on the Moon using India’s Chandrayaan 1 lunar orbiter in 2009. The water reserves could become a resource for future deep space exploration, offering breathable air for astronauts, water to drink and use, and fuel when its hydrogen and oxygen is liquefied. This potential, combined with the Moon’s proximity making it a technological catalyst, has led to nations around the world sending or planning to send a flurry of robotic and even crewed missions to Luna. In the long run, the Moon’s low gravity barrier, and its placement at the edge of Earth’s, could make it an efficient rocket platform for better, cheaper, faster deep space exploration, potentially even catalyzing human settlements across the Solar System.

Our Moon is valuable even beyond itself

Our serene, silvery cosmic companion’s value lies even beyond the exploration of itself in multiple more ways. Take a look at the following fantastic propositions our Moon offers. Who knows it might be useful during some policy debrief when people want to choose between the Moon and Mars based on logical fallacies tied to mutual exclusions? Our Moon is valuable even beyond itself:

  • As a unique platform for radio cosmology to study the Cosmological Dark Ages with missions on the Moon’s farside
  • To repurpose Moon missions for enabling deep space exploration
  • For leveraging Luna’s unique vantage point to monitor our Sun and its wind
  • As a geological time capsule and an age reference for Earth and events across the Solar System, as discussed above
  • By studying moonquakes and the lunar interior to understand the origin and evolution of solid surface planets & moons across our Solar System and beyond, as stated as well
  • As a well known, nearby reference body to calibrate imagers and radar systems for Earth observation as well as planetary exploration
  • For performing some of the most stringent tests of Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity using deployed retroreflectors
  • As a good proxy of solar and cosmic radiation in deep space environments to protect future astronauts exploring our Solar System, as mentioned above
  • With its regolith/soil being a layered record of our dynamic Sun over the last 2+ billion years, including of the interstellar mediums and environments our Solar System passed through in that time
  • Enabling an exclusive set of gravitational wave studies of highly energetic cosmic body collisions not possible to conduct from Earth or elsewhere in our Solar System
  • As a unique astronomy platform to study magnetospheres associated with exoplanets which are galactically nearby and potentially habitable
  • Perhaps, as a future launch base to other places in our Solar System

Taken together, the above aspects comprise a clear rationale not just for exploring our Moon but also standing up for its preservation against pure commercialization as well as national or private claims of ownership. Especially so when it’s the same kinds of exploratory technologies that both enable many of these fruits and can eventually destroy them.

Exploration ahead

The 382 kilograms of lunar samples which NASA astronauts brought to Earth during the Apollo missions revolutionized our understanding of our Moon and Earth’s formation, teaching us that our celestial companion very likely forged from the shards of Earth itself, after a protoplanet slammed into our planet about 4.5 billion years ago. In 2020 and 2024, China’s robotic Chang’e 5 and Chang’e 6 missions brought new lunar samples from unique sites, which have transformed our understanding of the Moon’s evolution by revealing complex events, especially for the lunar farside. What profound discoveries these are.

Going ahead, Chandrayaan 1’s discovery of lunar water at the poles has set the stage for adding a third dimension to our understanding of our Moon, Earth, and the Solar System. With upcoming surface rovers, robotic sample return missions like Chandrayaan 4, and new crewed missions from China as well as the US Artemis program exploring the unique but treacherous lunar south pole, we have the opportunity to study the Moon’s pristine water and mantle materials directly—both linked to Earth’s—and unravel not only key specifics about our Solar System’s history but fundamental formation mechanisms of Earth-and-Moon-like worlds across the Universe.

Look up at our Moon but also look up to it. It’s always around, always around for a nature profound to be found.

Poem: Always around

Gracious gray amid the blue & bright
Surreal silver against the night

Sometimes an uncanny crescent
or a gibbous glow in ascent

Other times a hollow halo
or a cloud glow

Reflective and rolling, when near
Stony stark skyline, when on it

Cosmic microcosm, when held
Enticing enigma, when leaving behind

This is our monumental Moon,
always around
for a nature profound
to be found

Always around,
always around for you
no matter the morning
it mourned through.

Poem notes: The Moon’s firm presence in our skies is cultural, enlightening, and aspirational. 🌖
