entry.title: Hijacking the PS5's RTMP Stream
entry.content:
The long way around to screen sharing.

Sony has progressively locked down what you can do with the PS5’s hardware. Streaming is a good example: the console gives you a nice, convenient “Broadcast” button, but the moment you want to do anything outside the handful of services Sony supports, it gets annoying very fast.

Third-party Bluetooth devices are the same story! Sony locks the wireless stack to their own peripherals, so your headphones or controllers from other brands simply won’t pair :/

#The Problem

I often stream games with friends on Discord who watch me play, but the PS5 doesn’t support screen sharing to Discord. The obvious fix is a capture card — plug the HDMI output into a capture card, feed it into OBS on your Mac, stream from there. But decent ones aren’t cheap, and I didn’t want to spend upwards of $100 just for this.

#Remote Play

Remote Play somewhat worked for me. I could connect the PS5 to my MacBook, share the Mac’s screen to Discord and play from there.

The problem is that you need to connect everything to the Remote Play device: controller, earphones, etc. I also occasionally ran into input lag, and the stream quality is entirely controlled by the PS5. You can’t really configure anything.

I didn’t want to change my physical setup every time I wanted to stream.

#How PS5 Streaming Works

The PS5 supports streaming to YouTube and Twitch by default if you’re signed into those accounts. The protocol used for this is RTMP, or Real-Time Messaging Protocol, which is commonly used for live audio/video streaming.

So when you start a broadcast, the PS5 roughly does this:

What if we could make our own device act as Twitch and receive that RTMP stream instead?

That’s the idea. The PS5 doesn’t hardcode Twitch’s IP, it looks it up via DNS every time. If we control what DNS returns, we control where the stream goes.

#Finding the Right Hostname

The obvious first attempt was to spoof ingest.twitch.tv directly. That’s the hostname the PS5 resolves when you hit broadcast, so pointing it at the Mac should work, right?

Not quite. ingest.twitch.tv:443 is actually a discovery endpoint, not the RTMP server itself. PS5 makes an HTTPS call to it asking “which regional ingest server should I use?” and Twitch responds with something like ap-southeast-1.prod.fi.contribute.live-video.net. Then the PS5 pushes the actual stream there.

Spoofing that hostname, I ran into a different problem: the actual Twitch ingest uses RTMPS (RTMP over TLS on port 443), and PS5 validates the certificate against trusted CAs. A self-signed cert doesn’t work, and there’s no way to install custom CAs on a PS5.

I then tried YouTube as a workaround. Its RTMP ingest uses plain RTMP on port 1935, so there was no TLS certificate to deal with. The PS5 happily sent the stream to my Mac, so I knew the basic approach worked.

The problem was that PS5 periodically checks YouTube’s API to make sure the stream is actually live. Since YouTube never received the stream, that check failed and it stopped broadcasting after about 60 seconds.

That meant I needed to find a Twitch endpoint that used plain RTMP. The answer came from watching DNS logs while broadcasting:

sudo tail -f /tmp/dnsmasq.log
# Sep 22 23:20:28 dnsmasq: query[A] ingest.global-contribute.live-video.net from 192.168.8.171
# Sep 22 23:20:28 dnsmasq: reply aps30.contribute.live-video.net is 35.55.13.0

The PS5 was resolving ingest.global-contribute.live-video.net, which chains down to aps30.contribute.live-video.net. That’s the real RTMP server. Spoofing contribute.live-video.net covers all subdomains and redirects the actual stream to the Mac without any certificate issues.

#DNS Trick

The setup has two main parts: dnsmasq and nginx-rtmp. I built a small macOS menu bar app that bundles both and manages them.

I run dnsmasq on my Mac and configure it to resolve Twitch’s ingest domains to my Mac’s LAN address:

server=1.1.1.1
server=8.8.8.8

# Redirect Twitch ingest traffic to the Mac
address=/contribute.live-video.net/192.168.8.175
address=/ingest.global-contribute.live-video.net/192.168.8.175
address=/live.twitch.tv/192.168.8.175
address=/live-sin.twitch.tv/192.168.8.175
address=/live-nrt.twitch.tv/192.168.8.175
address=/live-syd.twitch.tv/192.168.8.175
address=/live-fra.twitch.tv/192.168.8.175
address=/live-ams.twitch.tv/192.168.8.175
address=/live-lhr.twitch.tv/192.168.8.175
address=/live-jfk.twitch.tv/192.168.8.175
address=/live-lax.twitch.tv/192.168.8.175
address=/live-sea.twitch.tv/192.168.8.175

log-queries
log-facility=/tmp/dnsmasq.log

no-hosts
listen-address=0.0.0.0

192.168.8.175 is my Mac’s IP. When the PS5 asks DNS for one of these Twitch endpoints, dnsmasq returns my Mac’s IP instead. The PS5 connects to my Mac thinking it’s Twitch.

The last piece is pointing the PS5 at this DNS server. I have a GL.iNet router running OpenWRT, so I configured it to hand my Mac’s IP as the DNS server specifically for the PS5’s DHCP lease.

# SSH into the router and run:
uci add_list dhcp.lan.dhcp_option="tag:PS5,6,192.168.8.175"
uci commit dhcp
/etc/init.d/dnsmasq restart

The tag:PS5 part works because the PS5’s static lease already has that tag set in /etc/config/dhcp. Option 6 is the DHCP option for DNS server. The PS5 picks this up on its next DHCP renewal, no manual DNS configuration is required on the console!

#Receiving the Stream

For that, I’m using nginx-rtmp:

worker_processes 1;

error_log /tmp/nginx-error.log warn;
pid /tmp/nginx.pid;

events {
    worker_connections 512;
}

rtmp {
    server {
        listen 1935;
        chunk_size 4096;
        application ps5 {
            live on;
            record off;
            sync 10ms;
            # Notify our app when a stream starts
            on_publish http://127.0.0.1:9988/on_publish;
        }
    }
}

http {
    server {
        listen 8080;
        location /stat {
            rtmp_stat all;
        }
    }
}

The on_publish callback is how the menu bar app detects when the PS5 starts broadcasting. nginx fires a POST to localhost:9988 with the stream name, and the app surfaces the full RTMP URL ready to copy.

At this point, the PS5 is pushing its stream (1080p60, H.264, AAC stereo) directly to my Mac instead of Twitch.

From here I can pull the stream into anything: OBS to re-stream it, record it locally, or just play it directly.

#Watching It

Instead of going through OBS, I used mpv to pull the stream and shared the window to Discord. The low-latency profile keeps the delay less than a second:

mpv --profile=low-latency --audio-buffer=0.3 rtmp://127.0.0.1/ps5/stream-key

This has been quite reliable surprisingly. I’ve been using it for a few weeks now and haven’t had any issues. You can find the complete source code here.

Until next time! 👋

Have thoughts? Leave a comment at yashgarg.dev.

entry.title: Reflections from IndiaFOSS 2026
entry.content:
I attended IndiaFOSS 2026 this weekend (and Friday). I have been attending this festival (not a conference) since IndiaFOSS 2.0 in 2022. Every year the event keeps getting bigger. It's my favorite tech event of the year because of the people this event is able to bring together. It's always a joy reconnecting with old friends and meeting new FOSS hackers in the hallway.

This year felt a lot bigger. Felt, because when I told this to Rahul, he was quick to point out that this year only had 200 more checkins than last year. This is great, IndiaFOSS has really grown into a festival. There were so many wonderful booths. I only got to seeing a few of those because the talks and the people I was meeting in the hallway were super amazing and that's where my time went.

This delta is the visible effect of the hard work that the FOSS United team and volunteers are putting in. I keep discussing with Ansh about their sponsorship work. I saw the care and attention they put in maintaining relationships at my previous organisation Gooey.AI, who came back as a repeat sponsor this year. So did other organisations. This is despite the sponsorship being non-traditional. There are more verticals and efforts that I am less aware of where great, continuous improvement is happening: devrooms, public interest tech, 1-rupee fund, design & comms, student clubs, community partnerships, and so on. The organisation's actions carry the wisdom of the past several years.

OCaml Workshop

This year, I was attending with my team at FPL. Naturally, we ran an introductory workshop on the best programming language: OCaml. We did this on Friday, 25th September -- with Alina, Smayan, and Vimala.

Teaching is hard. What we presented as a 3-hour workshop was the product of several weeks of iteration and the labour of more than just the 4 of us. Having conducted and attended OCaml workshops earlier, this one was probably the smoothest. The notebook format we chose helped towards this in a couple of important ways:

  1. No installation needed: all attendees could work from their browser. While everyone had laptops, this meant that they could also do it on their phones if they wished. As KC mentions in the best talk of this event, earlier workshops have taken up to 1/3rd the allotted time just for installation. A standard environment solves this.
  2. Self-paced option: while we went over slides and asked attendees to scroll and solve exercises from time to time, attendees who wished to also had the option to read the material on their own and go faster than us. I saw a couple of attendees jump through to solving the games -- which was the last of our 4 sections. There are always a few advanced learners: I like this approach where they can go ahead and we as instructors focus on the average learner.

I also really liked our learners - there were about 25 of them and all of them sat through more than 3 hours of instruction. Some of the attendees - likely those who had seen some functional programming ideas before - were absorbing the concepts and solving exercises quickly. Most were slightly confused by the end and I could see the the mental homework they were carrying as they were saying their byes and leaving the room. This is great. This means we gave them something new to think about and they are in the process of learning.

That said, there are several places where we could've done better. In one of the more difficult exercises, I underestimated the difficulty of a solution and probably ended up passing my confusion on to one of the innocent learners. Exercises and their solutions can have badly written (confusing) code - especially when work gets offloaded to Claude. With some more improvements on our existing material, I think we can be even better at teaching OCaml to the average non-FP attendee.

With the volume of OCaml programmers that we have within our lab, and with who we are able to teach, I think we are working towards a small ecosystem in India that can support long-term projects written using OCaml and other related methodologies (for example, formal methods). I say this with the opinion that such techniques are here to stay alongside AI.

AI and teaching

A very interesting learning was how just bad Claude is at teaching. As I remember discussing later briefly with KC, this limitation has been faced by him and others too. I was reminded during our discussion that Khan Academy got access to GPT-4 (then the cutting edge) for a limited pilot program and not much has come out of it until now in terms of AI-generated content. I have reached a point where any "explanatory" text written by AI is immediately repulsive. Most AI generated READMEs are incomprehensible. The only place where I see it being useful for humans is when AI answers pointed questions with pointed answers. It is incredibly convoluted otherwise.

We had to do lots of re-writing in places where AI had generated examples. Maybe this will change but it is surely a hard problem.

Day 1

I got to meet ex-colleagues from my previous organisations -- Anand from Pipal, and almost everyone from Gooey.AI.

It was my time with Anand and at lambda retreat that drew me to functional programming first, where I met Sudha who initially mentored me through learning OCaml, and which led up to me working at FPLaunchpad now.

IndiaFOSS is also very much an excuse for meeting up with old friends who travel from different geographies and make time to be there :)

Favorite talks from Day 1:

  • KC's talk on OCaml notebooks: I am really liking this format for instructions. I have used browser-based instructional formats ([https://kaustubh.page/joy](for joy)) and seen Jupyter notebooks in action for this. x-ocaml notebooks that KC mentions in the talk are an improvement on both. I am sure that this format will catch on in other similar instructional formats.
  • Panel on DPI to PDI: This brought a unique format. I have done some work towards PDI with SAFAR, and some on PDGI. I really like their approach to solving problems.

TODO: add more thoughts on the DPI-PDI panel. more talks I liked from Day 1. then, about Day 2.

entry.title: IndiaFOSS 2026
entry.content:
IndiaFOSS is FOSS United's annual flagship conference. It aims to bring together India's technical community under one roof to discuss anything and everything Open Source. Its 2026 edition happened on 26th and 27th September and what a blast it was. Amazing talks, engaging booths, inspiring personalities, loads of random catchup, fascination, motivation, confusion, all together in a neat two day package! Let's unfold the same :)

First day

With heavy "first day, don't miss anything" motivation, I reached well before the Welcome Note. After fuelling ourselves with delicious breakfast and coffee, we headed straight towards Hall 3. This was the allotted room for Hardware and Compilers, Programming Languages and Systems tracks. I was super excited to find that we had Hall 3 booked this year, cause last year we were doing these devrooms in small classrooms. Those classrooms could barely fit 30-40 people inside it, and I missed few entire devroom tracks for the same reason.

Seeing the big hall made me super happy. I took my seat and was ready for the showdown. These were some of the talks I loved in the hardware track:

  • Build your own Open source keyboard with ZMK/QMK
    • Even though I love keyboards, I did not know a lot about building one from scratch. I have been a super happy frog clacking my Keychron K2V2 in this well.
    • Maybe just maybe it's time to build the dactyl I've always dreamed about.
  • CNC4Everyone
    • I entered this talk expecting to see a CNC machine like Jeff Gerling had shown few months ago, but to my surprise, this was a machine which works with cardboards!
    • There was one quote which was repeatedly used by the speaker: "China can fill a stadium with CNC operators and we won't fill a room". Keeping aside the national sentiments, I did not realize there were so few CNC operators in India. My friend's brother owns a CNC machine and I know a startup targeting CNC machine operators as their customer base! It could be a metaphor but I do think CNCs are more common than the speaker seemed to think.
  • My zero-to-hero journey deploying a fiber-optic and wireless community mesh
    • This was easily one of my favorite talks. This guy has peak FAFO energy!! I have a personal respect for people who go out there and just figure stuff out. No overthinking about consequences or how hard it would be, none of that matters.
    • In this talk Kiran talked about his experience trying to connect a secluded farmland he owns with WiFi. A bunch of his friends pooled in money and bought a farmland in the middle of nowhere and now for some reason they want WiFi there. While most of us would have given up, Kiran talks about how he got an uplink from BSNL there and connected sparse houses on the farmland with fiber optic cable. As the cables aren't that long, he had to FAFO and almost deceive a lineman into Fusion splicing xD.
  • Building Open Source Music Hardware in India - Tarab Instruments
    • Another guy with peak FAFO energy, but this time in music industry.
    • One of his slides said along the lines of: "Poverty is the mother of invention".
    • He talked about his journey of building musical instruments he absolutely adored but couldn't afford. So he decided to build his own! He described the complete process, his prototypes, tradeoffs in the current design and where he orders the parts from.
    • Another surprising point was the margins on these things! He completes the assembly at ~3k-ish and sells them from 10k! But he seems to hate making them and hence urged the audience to build it on their own from his github repo 🙃.

Next was the Compilers, programming languages and systems devroom after lunch! Honestly I believe they should have organized this in the morning, with topics so deep, one needs a lot more focus. This was made worse by the extra rice I was served inspite of giving a small pinch hand sign. So after a few talks: insulin went 📈, eyelids went 📉. 😭

  • Semantic Quantization in KV Cache Eviction
    • This sounded super interesting as I have recently found myself fascinated by the inner workings of LLMs.
    • It would have been amazing, except that it was full of math formulas. I didn't understand majority of it, but the simplified graphical representations of eviction policies were easy to grasp. And the results at the end showed impressive numbers. I am motivated to understand his findings in detail.
  • Bend, don't Break. Modern Techniques for Flexibility in Strongly Typed Functional Programming
    • This was a talk from FP India's Organizer Anupam. Another lively man who loves FP!
    • FPIndia is one of my favorite meetups to attend in Bengaluru, and I always look forward to Anupam's talks, naturally this was an awesome one :).
  • Benchmarking can be hard, here's why we're still creating a new one for OCaml
    • Oh boi, benchmarking is super super hard. People don't realize just how hard it is to craft fair benchmarks. It is very easy to go wrong or game them. There's a reason database industry loves dissing on each other's benchmarks. Most of them are incorrectly and unfairly crafted, and even the ones which try to do a fair comparison, fail often due to loads of minute details. Two minute silence in memory of PlanetScale TPCDS benchmark fiasco.
    • Well, this talk didn't invent some magic pill to fix it and mostly discussed what a good benchmark means.
  • What LLVM Does Differently When The Target Is CPU VS GPU
    • I am not an expert on LLVM internals, except knowing just enough from attending LLVM Social regularly. I think this is a blessing in disguise cause this way I am always excited by talks around these topics!
    • No doubt I enjoyed this one too. cuda-oxide's recent announcement has got me super excited to mess around with Rust and GPU on my Linux system!
  • PythonBPF - now with loops, custom funcs, and more maps!
    • eBPF is too close to my heart, I have been doing local propaganda of it ever since it's inception. Restricted but arbitrary code running inside kernel, I am in!
    • While I have not played with PythonBPF personally ( I am more of a Rust guy ), it was inspiring to see two students maintaining such an important library independently.
    • Also their snake game demo with state in kernel was cool!

I had to escape the devroom after these talks cause I was embarrassed of nodding off. I needed a break from talks, so I headed straight to Failures Mode Group gathering. This is an informal meetup which happens at IndiaFOSS every year, where we mostly hang out and talk about our self-hosting setups. While this is not my area to shine (soon I will get a VPS to get started!), Yash just bulldozered over everyone's setup. Buddy was collecting aura points and definitely won over some fans on that day xD.

We went around some booths and called it a day with a plan to visit a nearby cafe with whole herd of random mismatched groups: FP India + Rust India + BangPypers + PyCon India organizers. It was fun catching up with everyone and promising to meet next year again 😭.

Second day

On the second day, we got a bit late to arrive at the venue. We were afraid we would miss the breakfast, but were luckily just in time. Though we did end up getting late for the talks cause of an amazing catch up with Vishal. I had last talked with him two years ago I believe and had no idea he was doing such amazing philanthropy work in Bihar.

He mentioned how he has also worked for FREE for long periods of time just so that he can help government implement government programmes effectively on the ground. Sadly, government is not interested to improve their systems, they are content sitting in their AC rooms doing nothing :(. He is currently focusing most of his time in educating kids in a rural village. All the best dude, I hope all your work for this good cause comes to fruition!

After this uplifting conversation, we headed straight to the security devroom!

  • Reverse Engineering the PAN QR Code
    • Another Indian government expose session, author basically disproved India government claims of PAN card being encrypted and certified.
    • Author disproved the fact by building an open source scanner of the rather closed source government approved module. Except for the incompetence part, I found the reverse engineering journey super interesting!
    • I also found it rather uplifting that author started his journey after attending Nemo's talk last year on building an Open Source UPI app! Captain keeps on inspiring the next generation 🫡
  • When NO_PROXY Lies: Finding an IPv4-Mapped IPv6 Patch Bypass in Axios
    • I am a super surprised to find the root cause of this vulnerability, why tf are networking related libraries still parsing and comparing IP addresses using string comparisons!!???
    • Can't even call it Javascript ecosystem slop cause the same vulnerability was found in coturn too 🫠.
  • Extracting AES Keys from Embedded Devices Using Open Source Hardware
    • Anything power analysis is a treat for my brain by default
  • The Art of Userspace Sandboxing on Linux
    • This was the only talk in the security devroom with no live demos. While others loathed the sudden shift in atmosphere, I felt just at home!
    • I am accustomed to the talks where author does not give a shit about making eye candy slides cause he was busy doing the technical work! I personally try to always go for more eye candy and memes, etc but I am definitely not averse to such presentations :).
    • This was a good overview of the sandboxing landscape and even scraped some internal details at various points.
  • Keeping an Eye on your Eye: Disassembling and Reassembling Smart Camera Hardware to breach YOUR Security
    • This talk was an absolute chaos, both of the speakers were visibly very excited to deliver the talk and hence decided to do live desoldering on the stage 😭. Buddy was inhaling solder fumes without protection 💀. I texted on an internal attendee group applauding their guts to do a live demo of this, considering people have started showing recordings even of software demos cause demo gods aren't happy most of the times! Well, even for them, demo gods weren't in the mood on that day and crashed the laptop 😂.
    • All the chaos aside, they were blessed with some overtime and showed a glimpse of what they were going to present further on the firmware reverse engineering part. I found that really interesting and I still wished they could have just spent all their time in that section rather than trying the desoldering stunt :(.
  • Hacking India's Largest Exam System
    • A BANGER talk from a 19 year old who just happened to know a few things about computers and put them to good use! A typical "FBI Most Wanted" hacker origin story xD.
    • Even if you're not chronically online you would know about whole CBSC and CJP fiasco. This was the start of it all. Again, saddest part is government not admitting they have messed up big time and the absolute peak of skill issue by rebuilding the website multiple times and still getting hacked by the most basic exploits!

After the security devroom, we decided to attend this panel discussion around future of FOSS, SWE and Technical Education. Of course it was all going to be about LLMs. LLMs this, LLMs that, it was SO depressing! I had forgotten why I had stopped opening threads discussing LLMs on hackernews and lobsters. I am happy in my own little bubble, please don't try to pressure burst it till actual economic collapse happens. All the doomers read this.

In the second half, we went booth hopping, this time we had some amazing talk with Dev from Gooey.ai team, Anoop from Bruno, Raghav and Arun! After yapping all around, we headed for the Communi-Con. This was mini conf with lightning talks which community voted on! We enjoyed talks discussing postmarketOS, smartphone self-hosting, elixir, modern Javascript bloat hate, improvements to IndiaFOSS, etc.! All of this was made even more fun by an accompanying website which had live voting :P .

Another talk I really enjoyed was discussing WiFi setup of this conference, this was hands down the best WiFi setup I have seen in any conference. They had setup 1.X auth with loads and loads of routers and switches to ensure whole venue (even toilets, I checked 😂) had amazing connection, hats off to the team!

As an after conference ritual, I again ended up hanging out with FP and Rust India folks accompanied by Harsh, Yash and Sohom.

Booths

Across both days, I spent more time at the booths than before, that's how I ended up talking to Anoop and Dev xD. But having done a setup 2 years ago for Rust India, I know it is really tiring! I didn't get to enjoy the conference and just hated the whole experience. This is part of the reason we don't organize Rust India booths anymore :p. To respect their time, I went around with Yash and the people running the booths were lovely! Booths have definitely evolved over the last year, now we have games, a LOT MORE merch, etc.

  • Data For India had a nice guessing game with coins, stickers and highlighters to guess different domain statistics of India!
  • There were some students from school, who I instantly ran over to encourage! I had a good time interacting with them but also instantly felt like an uncle, I still remember how different adults used to visit student setup booths in science fair 😭.
  • There was a booth for FDroid too! Harsh was too shy to grab some stickers from the booth, so I had to sneak some out xD.
  • There were booths of all the major Linux distributions! Debian, Fedora, OpenSuse, Redhat, etc etc. I was surprised realizing all of them had an active community in Bengaluru!
  • There was also a booth of Tangled. After watching their Communi-Con talk and exploring it a bit more, I am feeling super bullish on them. They even support jujutsu out of the box!!
  • I also loved the idea of Hardware Showcase room, there were so many interesting projects in there. Someone had built an arcade machine at home 😮.
  • Kiran from the fiber talk above also had a booth. Yash spent A LOT of time and I really wished I had too. Look (image above) at all the cool gadgets he had. Btw this was like 5% of the total things he had, buddy was packing SO MUCH MORE!
  • Another club I didn't know about was Creative club, they meet regularly and collectively build and discuss their creative coding endeavours!
  • There was an OSM booth, always a big supporter of theirs 🫡.

Amazing side items I liked:

There were some details I liked and want to list without discussing:

  • Both days had different set of booths, this allows everyone to enjoy conference and give participants a chance to enjoy more diversity!
  • Absolutely loved the idea of Communi-Con, please please continue it!
  • 8+ devroom tracks this time, this is up from 2-3 last year. Absolute gold decision.
  • They decided to change the menu for second day's breakfast and lunch. Last year it was the same on both days.
  • Kept stumbling randomly into IndieWebClub folk.
  • Devrooms are handled by community, FOSS United team can focus on providing good framework, while actual domain experts do the amazing talk curation, recipe for amazing success!
  • Good T Shirt design.
  • Tiered ticketing system which allows earning individuals to help discount student tickets :).

Looking forward:

Few things I am looking forward to!

  • In Shree's lightning talk he mentioned some points which got me super excited for the next edition!
    • FOSSDEM style conference: OH MY GOD, this is the holy gold standard for me
    • 20+ devrooms: YES YES, you get the idea
    • Moving out of Nimhans as a venue: We need a good university with lots of decently sized classrooms
    • Main track getting shrinked: Main hall was empty most of the time, convert the general track in a devroom and allot it a smaller space
    • Even cheaper tickets for students and diversity scholarships: Respect++
  • Less LLM slop talks. Devroom organizers did an awesome job curating high quality talks, but some bad apples still slipped through the cracks :(.

Things to improve personally:

I would like to do a few things better next year:

  • I want to network with a LOT MORE strangers.
  • Check schedule thoroughly. Only after the conference I realized I missed a talk from a college junior of mine 😓.
  • I want to interact with the speakers whose talks I liked. This time I missed interacting with Kiran and Raunak.
  • I want to visit every single booth next year, I somehow missed Diagram Chasing and Bengawalk booths, thanks to Adithya for pointing they even existed!

Photo

And finally, a photo of Yash, me and Harsh (in that order) at IndiaFOSS. ( Nice try Tanvi . I am sure you will get the horns right in 2027 😂 )

P.S. Thanks to Yash for almost all the photos, sorry no sorry 🙈.

See you all in IndiaFOSS 2027!!

entry.title: Weeknote September 21 - September 27 2026
entry.content:
Whooo what a week it has been!

I know it sounds exciting and in some ways it has been.

Jobhunting proceeds as usual, and I am applying for whatever comes my way. Hoping that I get employed soon~ish because I have expensive tastes :P

I'm still working on my personal website. It's mostly done and I'll share it with the club and gather some feedback.

The shiny new allure of the potential project is always on the horizon.

I know it seems like I have paused the GTA game dev series for a bit but it's with good reasons mostly the job search and website development. Now that the website is almost finished we will be back soon.

Speaking of Gamedev. I had the pleasure of co-hosting a fun interactive podcast with my new friend Ishan. He reached out on the group about hosting a podcast showcasing and championing Indian Indie Devs and we had a conversation.

I'll share the first ep of that when it's out. Look forward to that!

Let's see what else. The highlights were shared above so now let's see the lowlights or real life bloopers.

I spent some time talking with the person whom I thought was interesting. I asked her out and she was receptive. Unfortunately (for me) she was in another country at the time vacationing for her birthday week.

When she got back because of various circumstances we couldn't go out on a date and she ended up ghosting me which I felt bad about. It's so interesting how human interactions over text are so ambiguous. One day you're liking each other's stories to show you're interested and the next you're seenzoning texts. Phones have become such a core part of the modern courtship experience and it's horrible. I wish that we had more third spaces which are safe and inexpensive where people who are single could interact with intention.

I saw something about how in Finland single people can signal that they are interested in a relationship in a grocery store by using a pink shopping cart and that's so clear. Please god of if I had one wish it would be make dating less ambiguous!

Such is life. What can ya do?

entry.title: IndiaFOSS 2026
entry.content:
About a year and a half ago, Nikhil showed me Nathan's blog post about IndiaFOSS 2024, we ended up going in September 2025 and it was cooler than the blog post made it out to be.

This was about a week or so after we founded ATLAS, and we had such an incredible time there. Talented and passionate people everywhere, students just like us and communities that were so aligned with everything we wanted ATLAS to be.

IndiaFOSS 2026 had such a bizarre contrast compared to last year. Over the past year, so many incredible people from different pockets of the Bengaluru tech scene assembled in one spot. Old friends from the last IndiaFOSS, friends from IndieWebClub, Homebrew and amFOSS along with Nithitsuki's assorted friends from threadlocked.

Another cool thing about this year is that ATLAS has grown into a solid community of people interested in tech. The last year we had about 4 or 5 people with us at IndiaFOSS. This year from a single message in our group chat, over 30 people had come in from our college alone. I'm really happy to see so much enthusiasm for the things that I love about tech.

Of all the people I got to see again, I was incredibly excited to meet Aman and Vonter from Diagram Chasing. We met Aman and Vivek in the last IndiaFOSS, where we talked about their incredibly cool work around building data stories and our (at the time) tiny college webring. My personal favourites from their already incredible list of projects are How Bangalore Uses The Metro, CBFC Watch and Who Is My Neta?. Seeing them again was a genuine delight.

Shoutout to Abhyudhaya and the rest of the COSH team for setting up the network infra and showing us the behind the scenes for it all. They pulled an all nighter to set up access points all over the convention center so that attendees could have Internet access.

The biggest ROI I had last year was writing Emacs in the "Interested in..." field on my sticker badge. It was a slightly out there choice, and it got people asking me about it. I did a two-parter this time. I wrote in Emacs on day 1 and Pantheon on day 2. The goal was that I'd attack two different groups that I was interested in getting to know. It was only after I wrote out Pantheon that Nikhil told me that people might assume I'm talking about the ElementaryOS desktop environment rather than the excellent science fiction show that I am currently obsessed with. Shoutout to Mukesh for validating me and talking about the show.

Talks

  1. KC's talk on building runnable textbooks - The idea itself inspires me. The biggest roadblock we keep thinking about while running events is the setup time. Removing that burden so that the attendees can simply get to learning the thing they wanted to learn sounds very useful to setup.
  2. Building tech communities that thrive - Lots of things to think about from this session, as one of the leaders in a student community myself.
  3. Modern techniques for flexibility in strongly typed functional programming - This talk had so much FP fanservice, The speaker managed to hit all the FP catchphrases ("Parse don't validate", "Making invalid states unrepresentable", etc.) and I love massaging my types. Nikhil and I had a lovely conversation with Anupam afterwards.
  4. Shaili Sanchaya - One of the things I'm very interested in is preservation. There are so many infinities to capture in our time here on Earth and I have so much respect for anyone taking the time to preserve and modernize things from the past. This talk was about a pipeline for transcribing old Kannada manuscripts and building out OpenType fonts for the language.
  5. Bezier Curves in GTK - Aman is a friend, so I couldn't not go to his talk. The talk was so worth it, it managed to straddle the line between unhinged and informative effortlessly.
  6. Seqout - A talk delivered by a friend, Mukesh. Always cool to see how you can adapt lessons and methods from other domains and solve problems for people that way.

The IndiaFOSS organizers did a fun thing this year with the last leg of Day 2, Communi-Con. A bunch of ten minute talks that were chosen by popular vote. I really like the idea because the talks themselves feel like they have significantly lower stakes than a talk you need to prepare for months for. I think I speak better off the cuff than when I rehearse endlessly and get all in my head about what to say.

Booths

I didn't get a chance to visit all the booths like I did last year, but here are my personal highlights:

  1. Diagram Chasing - The booth had a cool quiz and a lovely set of cards from their projects. I bought the Diagram Chaser's guide and Aman was kind enough to give me the Namma Metro stat card.
  2. Bengawalk - They had a cool map of all the BMTC bus routes and the positions of each bus. I am a huge fan of their work. Their work on YouTube was one of the first things that truly radicalized me about how much better my city can be.
  3. Absurd Industries - I loved the lightsaber. One of the main things I wanted to see from Nathan's blog post that I finally got around to seeing.

Overall, I had a blast. Getting to meet people who are on your wavelength, all concentrated in one place. Seeing old friends and other cool hackers who inspire us and were inspired by us all in one place. I will remember this IndiaFOSS even more fondly than the last one, and I genuinely cannot wait for the next one, hopefully with a booth or a talk (no promises of course).

P. S. At the end of day 1, we went to Bengaluru Cafe, which was a couple kilometres away. Pretty great dosa and coffee, just don't expect to be able to sit down and eat peacefully.

entry.title: Weeknote 39 2026
entry.content:
A super hopeful and super depressing week in the same. I seriously don't know what to do next because I was planning something major for my life and worked REALLY REALLY hard for it, but LUCK, LUCK, WHAT THE FUCK, why couldn't you on my side this time!? After I had ruled out all the possibilities of the failure, had put in the hours, had made sure I would not trip on even the most minute details, why did it have to be my bad luck which tripped me over at the end. I need to figure out what step to take next, its confusion all the way down.

Life

College friends

On Sunday morning, I met couple of my college friends. We went to Cubbon Park for a refreshing morning stroll. Amidst the stroll we talked about a lot of instances from our college days, some I knew about, some I didn't, some I wish I knew earlier about and some I wish I would have never know 😂. It's always fun to catch up with these dumbos :P. I also learnt one of them is now employed by SpaceX working on LLM inference!!?? That's bonkers crazy considering they don't have a team in India and this guy is working from Bengaluru itself. It's well deserved though, he is one of the smartest and most hard working person I know, hardwork + natural talent is a deadly combination.

After recharging our souls and draining the energy, we had a good replenishing breakfast in The Fresh Factory. Mann, this place is super expensive but serves amazing food!

Peter ki billi

I recently discovered Peter Cat Recording Company and have been completely hooked to their songs. So much so, I am writing this weeknote while enjoying We are getting married in the background.

Hmmm...this makes me realize that I am not able to enjoy the song cause I am focusing on typing and singing out loud at the same time, which is kinda bad multitasking.

Okay, turned off the song, so we were talking about this band, god bless my friend who told me about these guys, they compose songs with such delicacy, you feel bliss in every second. Bismillah has no bad songs, whole album is a fucking masterpiece. My stats of this band is higher than Snoop's average day. In fact, they have been promoted to my offline collection in the mobile and my FLAC collection. Portrait of time only has few songs I liked, and BETA is literally a beta album, I don't think I like any song from that album :(.

There is a sister band of this called Lifafa, I am yet to explore it, but having enjoyed few of it's song in the long drive, I do have high hopes from it too :).

Dead Thursday night

I had been feeling thorny in my throat since Wednesday but everything went absolute south on Thursday night when a mosquito woke me up just after one hour of sleep and then my fever plus cough took over the transfer of responsibility to keep me up for the rest of the night. I was already super pissed and just then I got the worst news at 3 AM. It's related to the opening paragraph above, and I just broke down at that point. I felt absolutely devastated. FUCK THIS SHIT.

My fever got washed down in the absolute rain of tears and my mind finally gave up at 6 AM. I did not realize when I fell asleep. I woke up at 12 PM and rushed to the office cause I wanted to offload this heavy heart to a friend.

If you find me talking about it right now, I might seem laughing it off, but internally I am completely broken, this was just unfair. I really wished I could give more details about this here right now, but I need some time to process it properly and plan the next step. I would unfold details about the incident in a future separate blogpost which is in work right now!

Zaitoon aflatoon?

I caught up with Amogh, Harsh and Yash over dinner at Zaitoon. Restaurent review is in the food section. It's always fun to catch up with this bunch. Last I talked to Amogh was long long back, so there is so much more to talk with him, I need to get hold of him separately :P.

IndiaFOSS

I attended first day of IndiaFOSS on Saturday and it was amazing! Me and Yash spent all of the first half in Hardware devroom and OH BOI, both of us have left the room feeling super inspired to enroll in a makerspace immediately! I also caught up with so many from different groups, I met friends from failure mode meetup group, ex-colleague group, current colleague group, IndieWebClub group, FP India group and finally Rust India group, it was super fun to catch up with everyone! Awesome talks, good food and so many friends around, perfect recipe for a happy day.

Climbing

We are back to CLIMBING!!!!

All the excitement ends at this full stop. It was a depressing week in climbing too. I think all the fasting over two weeks affected my body pretty badly, I felt super weak for all the sessions and couldn't even complete all the level 5s.

Sunday

I started out doing level 3s and level 4s in the new set, which was 2-3 walls considering I had been away for a few weeks. Level 3s were easy, and level 4s weren't bad too, except this one purple colour route on overhang, honestly it took me way too many attempts and finally a plea of help to a fellow climber to shine his wisdom on me. Definitely not proud of the send 🙃.

With all the 4s done, I started eyeing overhang 5s. Ideally what should have been all sends, were in reality partial progress on all. But progress is progress and for first session after a break, it wasn't as bad.

Tuesday

Is what I thought....there is this one level 5 red, OH MY GOD, it is so infuriating. No one, literally no one in the gym is struggling on it's last move and here I am who spent WHOLE session just trying to do that single move. I figured out a good beta for the rest of the route, but I kept falling down on the last move over and over and over for 4-5 hours. Worst part is I held it just once while trying out the route from a middle section instead from the start. THAT, THAT one fluke fuelled my false hope to keep trying this tiring move for the rest of the session!

https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/0mhT4Fhzvzc?mute=1 https://www.youtube-nocookie.com/embed/cDZCf9v-AsI?mute=1

I finally gave up and tried another level 5 on semi-slab wall, turns out that was even harder than the red level 5 😭. I still managed to figure out a creative beta for one of the crux moves, leaving just two more moves, out of which one is the second crux move. I was out of gas after this and called it a day.

Thursday

"Today I am going to send this red level 5". Only thought in my mind at the start of the session. I decided to practice only the last section of the climb separately, it had to be wired in my brain. Out of 10-15 tries, I stuck it 3 times. It wasn't a majority number neither were the successful lands continuous. But as the move is tiring I decided to try the full route from the start, relying on that off chance that I land it once and can call the route DONE.

Sadly, that never came, I tried SO SO MANY times, but it just didn't land. WHAT AM I DOING WRONG!! I asked for some advice from experienced climbers around, but no one has been able to point out where I am falling short. It still is a project for me and I will return to it next week with more despise. 😠

Only positive event was, I did manage to send remaining level 5s in overhang and cave section. Sadly, forgot to take any videos for them :(.

To my surprise, there was one super nearby to my house! Madhu's Iyengar Bakery has amazing Chocolate Cream Bun and Dilpasand. DING DONG, and now is the time time for Fenil's controversial takes: these cream buns are much much better than VB Bakery. This is the hill I am willing to die on.

I had such high expectations of the food, but everything vegetarian we ordered was super average, actually on second thought much lower than average. Maybe the non-vegetarian food is better, but my vegetarian readers, I would suggest to avoid this place :(.

I had my periods this week.

I don’t have an internal clock or tracking, so they often arrive as visiting guests: “Oh we were visiting your friends in the neighborhood, and it’s been a month since I have seen you so here we are!”

On the night before my periods, I was reading an article [1] on Substack about unclenching. And I have long known clenching to be my default state. Eighty percent of my waking time, I am clenched, the article was a reminder and how it affects our body, I read half of it and fell asleep.

I woke up the next day with period cramps and decided to apply the article? And I am weirded out by it, that it worked?! I personally cramp a lot on my first day of periods, they are the worst and I hate them. They can be painfully debilitating at times. So I lied down and consciously relaxed my body and put my hand on my stomach, the self-touch was gentle, warm and caring and when the cramp came instead of fighting it internally, I let it through and it felt better. But when I was not paying attention I’d reflexively fight back the cramp making it worse, so it took me some time to relax and let it wash over me. It was good in a weird way.

Since the first day was a huge success and I was “filled” with weird wholesome feelings, next day I decided to work! And that backfired, as I was sitting on my desk and looking at the nvim code, I started to cramp real bad, I realised that while working I had started clenching again, which aggravated the cramps. I took a break and focussed once more on relaxing, which helped.

I was using a heat pad on the side, I have macho-ed through this for the past twenty-seven years of my life, I am gonna provide whatever help I can to my body.

My first experience of unclenching, I’d like to think of it as full body relaxing, was when I came back from Vipassana, my chest-support straps kept falling off my shoulders, which was weird because they could not all have worn out at the same time. I realised that my shoulders were relaxed, and the size of the strap was adjusted for tensed up state.

I know how weird it is say, but I had a good run of periods this time. Touchwood! I am planning to repeat this experiment and post an update.

Cheers,
Calra

P.S. a mini-rant (Note: this bit was added later in the article)
I hate how the period adverts when I was growing up were mostly around, wear these magical pads with wings and play all the sports, it is not impossible, but trust me, it’s very physically taxing especially in the first two days.  The body is still doing the hardwork, think if there were an advertisement for fever going like, “hey wear this icepack for fever and go play football!” the body is still exhausted, you can still play football but it is not recommended, it’s an exaggeration, I get it, but you must understand where I am coming from. I am sure, the original ads were trying to fight against the older traditions and taboos of “keeping women (read it as people who menstruate)  indoors”, reminds me of a line from A Room of One’s Own by Virginia Woolf, either women are treated as divine or inferior, protected, never just human. Sad.

entry.title: Tracking execution events for your WorkManager Workers
entry.content:
WorkManager is Android Jetpack’s first party solution to long-running background work. It takes care of dealing with the idiosyncrasies and differences between Android versions, and gives you a very simple API that lets you focus on what needs to happen instead of the how. It’s very well designed, and as someone who’s had to deal with JobScheduler and AlarmManager years ago for this class of problems, it’s a boon.

That said, debugging WorkManager is somewhat cumbersome (ref). This also had the limitation that it only lets you debug issues on your own device, and collecting metrics from the field required instrumenting each worker manually to report back metrics which just doesn’t scale all that well.

Enter: ExecutionEventListener. This is a brand new API that was introduced in WorkManager 2.12.0. The WorkManager team has also introduced a new work-analytics library on top of this low-level API to retrieve historical execution data, but we’ll focus on ExecutionEventListener. It is still experimental, so you’ll need to mark your code with @ExperimentalEventsApi.

As of writing, the API looks like this:

@ExperimentalEventsApi
public interface ExecutionEventListener {
    public suspend fun onStarted(workInfo: WorkInfo)


    public suspend fun onStopped(@StopReason stopReason: Int, workInfo: WorkInfo)


    public suspend fun onFinished(result: Result, workInfo: WorkInfo)


    public suspend fun onException(throwable: Throwable, workInfo: WorkInfo)
}

You start by creating a subclass of this interface, then pass it to your WorkManager Configuration.Builder like so:

WorkManager.initialize(
  application,
  Configuration.Builder()
    .setWorkerFactory(workerFactory)
    .setExecutionEventListener(WorkManagerExecutionTelemetry())
    .setMinimumLoggingLevel(Log.DEBUG)
    .build(),
)

I wired this up in my app Claw to emit events to Sentry, and can now visualize them via a dashboard to see data like failure rates and p50/p95 of execution duration. Here’s the relatively minimal dashboard I set up which has collected a couple of days of data through my internal testing channel.

Naturally with this still being a new API, there are some quirks to it. The major one is that while you get a ListenableWorker.Result instance in the method parameters, all three subtypes (Success, Failure, and Retry) are marked with @RestrictTo(RestrictTo.LIBRARY_GROUP) which means Lint flags any attempt to use them for determining what the result actually is. I’ve filed an issue to provide a solution for this. In the meantime, you can simply suppress the Lint like I do. Another problem is the lack of support for @IntDef and friends in Kotlin, which means the stopReason parameter arrives as a plain Int. When publishing this as a metric, you’ll have to check its values against the WorkInfo.STOP_REASON_* constants yourself and map it to a string.

You can find my implementation here which deals with both these paper cuts.

Thanks for reading!

entry.title: Waxing poetic about my records and turntable
entry.content:
Music in the streaming age is weightless. It reaches you through the aether from servers thousands of miles away into whatever speaker happens to be nearby. It seems almost infinite, is completely free of friction, and incredibly easy to take for granted.

I recently bought a record player and my first three records, with plans to buy more.

To anyone used to tapping a glass screen to hear any song ever recorded, this looks like too much work to listen to a limited number of tunes. Records are bulky, inconvenient, require physical storage, and only hold about twenty minutes of music per side before you have to get up and flip them over.

Yet, much like taking the time to manually grind whole coffee beans instead of stirring instant powder into boiling water, the friction adds to its appeal.

The instant coffee vs. freshly brewed coffee analogy breaks down when it comes to quality though. Any coffee connoisseur will say brewed coffee tastes better than instant (due to a variety of reasons), but standard CD-quality digital audio technically has higher fidelity and dynamic range than vinyl ever will. Records degrade over time due to dust and scratches, leading to sound artifacts (which I am coming to terms with), and cost a ridiculous amount of money in India, thanks to import duties and a weak rupee.

What makes a record “worth it”, still

I’m sort of a minimalist and never thought I’d have a collection of anything, but I love music and hate how exploitative streaming is (more on this later), so it makes complete sense to have a little record collection.

Here are some reasons I started one, in no particular order.

Difference from digital media

Unlike digital files which store sound as a collection of bits, a vinyl record is a direct physical artifact of audio.

When a record is pressed, soundwaves are literally etched into a single continuous groove on a sheet of PVC plastic. If you zoomed in with a microscope, you'd see the actual undulating shape of the soundwaves themselves.

It’s such a delicate, magical, yet simple thing, and it boggles my mind that this exists at all.

Relative rarity

Vinyl records went out of fashion because of their cost of production, fragility, and low portability, and everyone streams, so it makes the experience even more interesting, as I didn’t get to listen to any until recently. You did however see them in all sorts of media, especially that from the heyday of records, which added to the mystique.

The art looks really pretty

The sleeve, of course, has the album art, which is usually pretty enough on its own, but they also quite commonly have things like lyrics booklets,

Records themselves look good as well

Our first record, “Ali” by Vieux Farka Touré and Khruangbin, was a translucent blue-green instead of the usual black, which was such a pleasant surprise.

Another record I purchased, “Is This It” by The Strokes, is a limited editiion translucent red.

Plain black records also look great, though.

You might enjoy the music more

The ritual of pulling the disc from its sleeve, gently lowering the tonearm, and watching it spin anchors your attention to the room. It turns listening into a dedicated activity rather than background noise.

Dust and cat hair gets on the record, which causes pop sounds, and the act of moving it to and from the sleeves and the turntable creates static, which makes a sort of buzzing sound. This means you have to clean a record each time to get the debris out and remove the static. You really have to love a record to want to go through all of that. It connects you to the activity of listening instead of being a passive participant, and I guess the work makes you appreciate it more?

Streaming pays very little

The artist gets more money. If you buy a record in India, maybe 10% of the sale price has actually gone to the artist (because the retailer, the government, the publisher, etc all take their cut), but it takes 100,000 to 150,000 streams on Spotify for an artist to net the same amount. Streaming is hell for smaller artists especially, and is not enough to make a living.

A section of Wikipedia on Spotify’s compensation practices

More miscellaneous reasons

  • My partner’s cousins and brother have one.
  • It’s a physical display of your music tastes.
  • Actually owning your music.
  • Records and the turntable and other equipment look really good in a room, and you can talk about it.

Neighbourhood record store

I live quite close to this cute record store called On the jungle floor. They’ve got a massive collection of records and the staff is friendly. I love visiting there to just look at the really expensive equipment they have and drool at the LPs they have.

Two of the records we’ve bought have been from here!

An interesting thing I heard after a couple of conversations there with people either working or hanging out there as friends of the owner, people volunteer there for free for some reason? Not sure why anyone would do that other than as a favour to a friend. If any reader has done something like this for a for-profit business, please let me know.

There was a guy behind the counter who wasn’t an empployee. He’s a DJ and was playing some of his personal records from a massive tote bag full of records, trying to figure out what to play on his next set. Maybe he was getting the most out of the ₹3L turntable. I didn’t get to talk to him too much, but my partner really liked the LPs he had, and since we can’t find them for sale anywhere in India, this has caused a lot of consternation. For anyone who wants to check out his music, his name is Saksham, @ghewxr on Instagram.

The current rig

I’m using an almost entry-level turntable from https://www.headphonezone.in/, the AT-LP60X. It doesn’t have a lot you can mess with, for instance, it does not have an adjustable counterweight on the tonearm (the part that holds the needle), which means one less thing to mess with and mess up, in my opinion.

I just use a portable bluetooth speaker via aux at the moment because dumping all my disposable income into a new hobby would be silly. Even when I do get speakers, I’m going for the (relatively) cheaper end for now. I’m not an audiophile, and thank god for that. Like every hobby there’s a way to dump all your money into this. After a certain point, you get diminishing returns and are just trying to optimise the fun out of your equipment.

I’m thinking of doing listening parties, though, and the idea of bringing people over to listen to music coming out of a cheap portable speaker does seem a bit sad. Down the line, the goal is to set up a proper stereo amplifier connected to a decent pair of passive bookshelf speakers, preventing the speakers from turning the record’s stereo sound into mono, add more depth to the music, and fill my room. The bass on the Strokes album goes hard, so a subwoofer is also on the cards.

Thinking of getting the Polk Audio Monitor XT15 Speaker from avstore.in alongside the Fosi Audio V3 amplifier. This will go great with my HiBy music player as well (because of the aux input), letting me listen to digital music from a more “intentional” source than streaming from my phone.

entry.title: (#2026-W38) maps, comics, birbal and stickers
entry.content:
On Sunday, the chronicles of the long weekend continued. I went to the Museum of Art and Photography with Sumnima, where we went through the an exhibition called “A Moving Line: 1500 Years of Indian Visual Storytelling”. ¶

Now, don’t kill me, but this was my first time going to MAP after being in Bengaluru for four years. I probably have many Reels and links of this place saved, of exhibitions that have long come by and gone. MAP to me is one of those must-go places here, and so I was glad to finally do my MAP darshan with Sumi. ¶

I also want to mention that I really appreciate the accessibility of the whole place. A wheelchair ramp for the entrance, a lift big enough for even a motorized wheelchair to enter comfortably, and self-opening doors with key cards placed at a comfortable height. The staff was really helpful and friendly too. The place is well thought through. ¶

The exhibition itself was wonderful. We were in a quiet room with red walls, surrounded by artwork drawn over multiple decades. Historical prints existed in the same space as modern Indian creators, with even showcases of the adoption of language in visual art across the country. ¶

The part that I loved the most is the inclusion of Amar Chitra Katha. Growing up, I can’t remember a single comic I read that wasn’t under ACK’s umbrella of work —- except maybe Chacha Chaudhary from Diamond Comics, who was a travel partner on every train ride. The cartoons and their stories always lingered in my memory. ¶

But yeah, the exhibition had a complete wall of covers of ACK’s comics, including ones of Mahabharata, Lord Krishna’s Chronicles, and Akbar & Birbal. Man I love Birbal. Birbal is the coolest. They also had a vinyl of Birbal’s stories. Did I tell you I love Birbal? ¶

There was also this little leaflet in the centre of the exhibition, where you could complete a comic strip by drawing your own story. I drew from an epiphany that left me and Sumi laughing for a long time. You can ask me for it if we meet in person. ;) ¶

I don’t particularly remember how the Monday went by for me. I remember seeing a lot of my Marathi friends posting Stories from their Ganesh Chaturthi celebrations and I sent a mental prayer to all the pictures of idols too. ¶

I also undertook the surgical process of increasing the storage of my main partition on my laptop. I say “surgical” because I learned that the laptop makes a familiar beep every second when in recovery mode, similar to those patient monitors in hospitals. Not to say that they are the same thing, ofcourse. I feel like I have to disclose that stuff nowadays. The resizing was ultimately a success. ¶

Saturday was spent hanging out with the folks at IndieWebClub. The meetup this week was more development-related and set around digital housekeeping. I started out with the intention to work on my Nannoo’s website, but I quickly got absorbed in talking to many of the other attendees about their set tasks instead. ¶

I’ve sort of developed an appreciation for the ways in which people have come to use LLM’s. The technology itself is still as crude and intellectual theft-y as it has ever been, but these humans have come to utilize it in a way that brings their warmest ideas to life. ¶

Divjot recently shifted his Now page to look more like Orkut, while Arpit made a portal for the his wife’s monthly Bengali meal service. Jatan, who isn’t a programmer by profession, jailbroke his Kindle and fine-tuned his calm writing setup with help from LLM’s. I have some apps that I am working on myself, with the intention to ultimately spend less time on my devices. ¶

I don’t know, we might be able to abstract our way out of our technological pit and get back to our human connections. But there’s a lot of fascism to be cleaned up before we get there. ¶

That’s all the musing there is this week! I am getting very sleepy now. Sweet dreams, dear reader. ¶
